fuentes/tablillas-de-ebla/autor.texto: Scribes of the royal palace of Ebla

fuentes/tablillas-de-ebla/resumen.texto: Archive of up to 1800 complete tablets, 4700 fragments and thousands of chips, found in Palace G at Ebla by Paolo Matthiae and his team in 1974-1975. The destruction of the palace, around 2300 BC, baked the clay and preserved it.

fuentes/tablillas-de-ebla/por_que_import.texto: It is the main archive of the third millennium BC in the Levant: it documents the administration, trade, diplomacy and wars of Ebla with Mari and other cities.

fuentes/tratado-de-ebla-y-abarsal/resume.texto: Diplomatic treaty between the city-states of Ebla and Abarsal, signed around 2350 BC, proposed as the oldest recorded diplomatic treaty in history. It is not known where Abarsal was: Giovanni Pettinato prefers to identify it with the later Assur, although the text points to a state close to or bordering Ebla, and Tell Chuera has also been proposed.

fuentes/tratado-de-ebla-y-abarsal/por_qu.texto: It shows the level of written diplomacy in the Levant of the third millennium BC.

fuentes/tablillas-de-alalakh/resumen.texto: Sets of administrative and legal tablets from Alalakh, from levels VII (Middle Bronze Age) and IV (Late Bronze Age), with the records of the minor dynasty of Yamhad and of the kingdom of Mukish. After a gap of less than a century, the records reappear with the dynasty of Idrimi.

fuentes/tablillas-de-alalakh/por_que_imp.texto: They give the names of kings, vassals and officials and allow the organization of a Syrian kingdom of the second millennium BC to be reconstructed.

fuentes/estatua-de-idrimi/resumen.texto: Sculpture found at Alalakh by Leonard Woolley in 1939, from the 15th century BC, with a long autobiographical inscription in Akkadian of King Idrimi, now in the British Museum. It tells of Idrimi's flight from Aleppo, his life among the Habiru and his seizure of the throne of Alalakh.

fuentes/estatua-de-idrimi/por_que_import.texto: It is one of the few royal autobiographies of the Late Bronze Age in Syria. The date of the statue is debated, since it was found in a stratum several centuries later than Idrimi's life, and some date it to around 1400-1350 BC.

fuentes/archivo-de-qatna/autor.texto: Scribes of the royal palace of Qatna

fuentes/archivo-de-qatna/resumen.texto: Cuneiform tablets from the royal palace of Qatna, which mention King Idanda and show that the kingdom kept some autonomy in the 14th century BC. No archive of King Akizzi, whose letters were found at Amarna, has been found at Qatna.

fuentes/archivo-de-qatna/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main written source on Qatna in its last stage.

fuentes/tablillas-de-emar/resumen.texto: Archive of cuneiform tablets from the 14th to 12th centuries BC, found at Emar, with local documents in Akkadian and about 100 tablets in Hurrian and one in Hittite. It is the main source on the city within the Hittite sphere until its fall in 1187 BC.

fuentes/tablillas-de-emar/por_que_import.texto: It makes it possible to study life in a city on the Euphrates under the Hittites, through ritual, legal and administrative texts.

fuentes/textos-de-ugarit/soporte.texto: Clay tablets with alphabetic and syllabic cuneiform writing

fuentes/textos-de-ugarit/resumen.texto: About 1500 texts and fragments found at Ugarit and Ras Ibn Hani since 1928, written in Ugaritic, a previously unknown northwest Semitic language, as well as in Akkadian, Hurrian, Sumerian, Egyptian and Luwian. The texts from the palace libraries, a temple and private houses include epic poems, rituals, letters, legal texts and administrative lists.

fuentes/textos-de-ugarit/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most important source on Canaanite religion and society in the Late Bronze Age.

fuentes/ciclo-de-baal/resumen.texto: Ugaritic text of about 1300-1100 BC in six tablets (KTU 1.1-1.6) about the storm god Baal. The first two recount his struggle with the sea god Yam, the third and fourth the construction of his palace, and the last two his combat with Mot, death.

fuentes/ciclo-de-baal/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main known Canaanite mythological text and allows the myths of the Levant to be compared with those of the Tanakh.

fuentes/leyenda-de-keret/resumen.texto: Ugaritic epic poem of c. 1500-1200 BC about King Kirta of Hubur, son of the god El, who lost seven wives, lost his entire family and asks his father for an heir.

fuentes/leyenda-de-keret/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the three great Ugaritic poems and shows the royal ideology of the city.

fuentes/leyenda-de-aqhat/resumen.texto: Incomplete Ugaritic epic poem of the 14th century BC in which the hero Danel receives a son, Aqhat, from the gods; Aqhat is later killed by the goddess Anat.

fuentes/leyenda-de-aqhat/por_que_importa.texto: It is the third great Ugaritic poem, alongside the Baal Cycle and the Legend of Keret.

fuentes/himnos-hurritas-de-ugarit/resume.texto: Collection of music written in cuneiform on tablets found at Ugarit, from c. 1400 BC. One of them, almost complete, contains the Hurrian hymn to Nikkal, the oldest surviving substantially complete work of notated music.

fuentes/himnos-hurritas-de-ugarit/por_qu.texto: It allows the study of the oldest notated music and of the Hurrian connections of Ugarit.

fuentes/carta-de-ammurapi-al-rey-de-alas.texto: Letter from Ammurapi to the King of Alashiya

Letter from the last king of Ugarit, written in reply to the king of Alashiya, who had warned him of enemy ships. Ammurapi confirms that the ships arrived, that his cities were burned, and that his troops and chariots are in Hatti and his ships in Lukka.
It is the most cited contemporary testimony of the attacks that preceded the fall of Ugarit.

fuentes/cartas-de-rib-hadda/resumen.texto: About sixty letters from Rib-Hadda of Byblos to Pharaoh Akhenaten, among the Amarna letters, asking for military help against Abdi-Ashirta and Aziru of Amurru, who were taking coastal cities. In them Rib-Hadda invokes only the Lady of Byblos, and at one point he has to flee into exile in Beirut.

fuentes/cartas-de-rib-hadda/por_que_impo.texto: It is the main source on the struggles over the Lebanese coast during the reign of Akhenaten.

fuentes/cartas-de-rib-hadda/leer.0.titul.texto: Translation by C. R. Conder, The Tell Amarna Tablets (1893), now superseded, on Internet Archive

fuentes/cartas-de-abdi-heba/resumen.texto: Six letters from the local chief of Jerusalem to the pharaoh among the Amarna letters, written by the scribe of Jerusalem (EA 285-290). In them he denounces the pressure of the Habiru and of other Canaanite rulers and asks for troops or for an Egyptian commissioner to be sent.

fuentes/cartas-de-abdi-heba/por_que_impo.texto: They are the main written source on Jerusalem before the Iron Age.

fuentes/cartas-de-abdi-heba/leer.0.titul.texto: Translation by C. R. Conder, The Tell Amarna Tablets (1893), now superseded, on Internet Archive

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-288/resumen.texto: Letter from the local chief of Jerusalem to the pharaoh, titled «Benign Negligence», which reports, among other things, that Zimredda of Lachish died at the hands of the Habiru. It is preserved in the Vorderasiatisches Museum in Berlin.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-288/por_que_i.texto: It shows how the situation of the Canaanite cities under Egyptian rule looked from Jerusalem.

fuentes/cartas-de-labayu/resumen.texto: Three letters from the ruler of Shechem to the pharaoh, among the Amarna letters, in which he defends himself against accusations of rebellion made by other Canaanite kings. EA 254, titled «Neither Rebel nor Criminal (2)», is preserved in Berlin.

fuentes/cartas-de-labayu/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main source on the mountain kingdom of Shechem before Israel.

fuentes/cartas-de-abimilki-de-tiro/resum.texto: Ten letters from the prince of Tyre to Amenhotep IV, among the Amarna letters. In one (EA 147) the pharaoh confirms him on the throne after his father's death, and in another he calls him general (rabisu). Half of the letters deal with Zimredda of Sidon.

fuentes/cartas-de-abimilki-de-tiro/por_q.texto: It is the source for the life of Tyre and for the rivalries of the Phoenician cities in the 14th century BC.

fuentes/cartas-de-los-reyes-de-gezer/tit.texto: Letters of the Rulers of Gezer

fuentes/cartas-de-los-reyes-de-gezer/res.texto: Letters of Milkilu, Adda-danu and Yapahu, the three rulers of Gezer (Gazru) in the Amarna letters, some with complaints against other cities and some with oaths of loyalty. There is a letter from the pharaoh to Milkilu (EA 369) and five letters from Yapahu (EA 297-300 and EA 378).

fuentes/cartas-de-los-reyes-de-gezer/por.texto: They document the internal politics of the Canaanite cities of the Shephelah.

fuentes/cartas-de-akizzi-de-qatna/resume.texto: Several letters from the king of Qatna to the pharaoh, among the Amarna letters, asking for help against invaders. They were found in the Amarna archive, not in Qatna.

fuentes/cartas-de-akizzi-de-qatna/por_qu.texto: They show the Hittite advance into Syria as seen from a vassal kingdom of Egypt.

fuentes/cartas-de-aziru/resumen.texto: Letters from Aziru of Amurru to the pharaoh, among the Amarna letters, in which he protests his loyalty to Egypt. Rib-Hadda of Byblos accuses him, in his own letters, of taking coastal cities.

fuentes/cartas-de-aziru/por_que_importa.texto: They show Amurru's move from the Egyptian orbit to the Hittite one.

fuentes/cartas-de-alashiya/titulo.texto: Letters from the King of Alashiya to the Pharaoh

fuentes/cartas-de-alashiya/resumen.texto: Letters from the king of Alashiya (Cyprus) to the pharaoh, among the Amarna letters, dealing with Alashiyan copper and with requests for silver and ivory in exchange. One of them mentions 500 talents of copper, about 12.5 tonnes, and apologizes for having sent so little.

fuentes/cartas-de-alashiya/por_que_impor.texto: It is the main source on the international trade in Cypriot copper in the Late Bronze Age.

fuentes/libro-de-josue/resumen.texto: Sixth book of the Hebrew Bible, the first of the Deuteronomistic history, which recounts the campaigns of the Israelites in Canaan, the destruction of their enemies and the division of the land among the twelve tribes. Scholarship considers it historically problematic: the conquest as it is narrated is not a historical event, and archaeology indicates a gradual emergence of Israel within Canaanite society.

fuentes/libro-de-josue/por_que_importa.texto: It is the source of the tradition of the conquest of Canaan, written centuries after the events it recounts, and it forces a distinction between the biblical account and what archaeology shows.

fuentes/libro-de-josue/leer.0.titulo.texto: Book of Joshua in the King James Version, on Wikisource

fuentes/libro-del-exodo/resumen.texto: Second book of the Torah, which narrates the departure of the Israelites from Egypt, the giving of the law at Sinai and the construction of the tabernacle. It was composed over several centuries, and its relationship to a specific historical event is debated.

fuentes/libro-del-exodo/por_que_importa.texto: It is the source of the exodus tradition; scholars debate whether there was a historical event behind it and how large it was.

fuentes/libro-del-exodo/leer.0.titulo.texto: Book of Exodus in the King James Version, on Wikisource

fuentes/libro-del-genesis/resumen.texto: First book of the Torah, which includes the accounts of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, among them their journeys through Canaan and to Egypt. It was composed centuries after the events it recounts, and no contemporary inscriptions naming the patriarchs are known.

fuentes/libro-del-genesis/por_que_import.texto: It is the source of the patriarchal tradition; it serves as evidence of later Israelite memory, not of the period it narrates.

fuentes/libro-del-genesis/leer.0.titulo.texto: Book of Genesis in the King James Version, on Wikisource

fuentes/yon-la-ciudad-de-ugarit/titulo.texto: The City of Ugarit at Tell Ras Shamra

fuentes/yon-la-ciudad-de-ugarit/resumen.texto: Synthesis of the French excavations at Ugarit, with the palace quarter, the temples, the houses and the archives.

fuentes/yon-la-ciudad-de-ugarit/por_que_.texto: It is a reference for the topography and history of Ugarit.

fuentes/watson-wyatt-handbook-of-ugariti.texto: Wilfred G. E. Watson and Nicolas Wyatt (eds.)
Collective handbook on the kingdom of Ugarit, its language, script, literature, religion and history.
It is a reference in Ugaritic scholarship.

fuentes/moran-cartas-de-amarna/resumen.texto: Translation and edition of the Amarna letters, with introduction and notes, used as the reference edition.

fuentes/moran-cartas-de-amarna/por_que_i.texto: It makes it possible to read the letters of the Levantine rulers and their correspondence with the Egyptian court.

fuentes/rainey-la-correspondencia-de-el-.texto: Critical edition of the Amarna letters, with translation and a study of the grammar of the language of the Canaanite letters.
It is the edition of the letters of the Canaanite rulers with the most linguistic detail.

fuentes/mazar-arqueologia-de-la-tierra-d.texto: Archaeology of the Land of the Bible, 10 000-586 BC
Archaeological synthesis of Palestine and Israel from the Neolithic to the fall of Judah, with chapters on the Early, Middle and Late Bronze Age periods.
It is a reference for the chronology of the strata of the southern Levant.

fuentes/finkelstein-silberman-la-biblia-.texto: Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman
Work that contrasts the biblical account with archaeology, from the patriarchs and the exodus to the conquest and the monarchy. It argues that Israel emerged gradually within Canaanite society.
It is a reference for the position that denies a conquest of Canaan as the book of Joshua tells it.

fuentes/knapp-arqueologia-de-chipre/titu.texto: The Archaeology of Cyprus: From Earliest Prehistory through the Bronze Age

fuentes/knapp-arqueologia-de-chipre/resu.texto: Archaeological synthesis of Cyprus up to the end of the Bronze Age, with the Philia culture, the Late Bronze Age centres, copper metallurgy and trade with the Levant and the Aegean.

fuentes/knapp-arqueologia-de-chipre/por_.texto: It is the general reference for Cypriot sites and chronologies.

fuentes/potts-el-golfo-arabigo-en-la-ant.texto: History of the Arabian Gulf in two volumes: the first runs from prehistory to the fall of the Achaemenid Empire and includes the chapters on Dilmun, Magan and the Hafit, Umm an-Nar and Wadi Suq cultures; the second runs from Alexander the Great to the arrival of Islam. The first volume is cited as 1990 and as 1992, depending on the edition.
It is the main synthesis on eastern Arabia in the Bronze Age.

fuentes/archi-ebla-y-sus-archivos/titulo.texto: Ebla and Its Archives: Texts, History, and Society

fuentes/archi-ebla-y-sus-archivos/resume.texto: Study of the texts of the Ebla archive and of the history and society of the third-millennium BC kingdom, written by one of the archive's epigraphists.

fuentes/archi-ebla-y-sus-archivos/por_qu.texto: It is the reference on the internal chronology of the first kingdom of Ebla.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-35/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 35 (The Hand of Nergal)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-35/resumen.texto: Letter from the king of Alashiya (Cyprus) to the pharaoh, titled «The Hand of Nergal», of thirteen paragraphs on the obverse and reverse.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-35/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the letters from the king of Alashiya to the pharaoh about copper and the relations between the two kingdoms.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-38/resumen.texto: Letter from the king of Alashiya, titled «A Brotherly Dispute», of six paragraphs, with much of the reverse left unwritten.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-38/por_que_im.texto: It shows the tone of equality between the king of Alashiya and the pharaoh.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-147/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 147 (A Hymn to the Pharaoh)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-147/resumen.texto: Letter from Abimilki of Tyre, titled «A Hymn to the Pharaoh», twin of EA 149, which seems to precede it. In it the pharaoh confirms Abimilki on the throne of Tyre.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-147/por_que_i.texto: It is the most cited of the Tyrian letters among the Amarna letters.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-161/resumen.texto: Letter of eight paragraphs, titled «An Absence Explained», preserved in the British Museum; it was written by Aziru of Amurru.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-161/por_que_i.texto: It is one of Aziru's letters to the pharaoh.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-245/resumen.texto: Fourth of five letters from Biridiya, ruler of Magidda (Megiddo), titled «Attribution of Blame»; it is in good condition apart from a fragment of the lower right corner.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-245/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the letters from Megiddo to the pharaoh.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-252/resumen.texto: Letter from Labaya of Shechem to the pharaoh, titled «Forgiving the Enemies», written on the obverse, the lower edge and the reverse.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-252/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the three surviving letters of Labaya.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-286/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 286 (A Throne Granted, Not Inherited)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-286/resumen.texto: Letter from Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem, titled «A Throne Granted, Not Inherited», one of the six written by the scribe of Jerusalem.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-286/por_que_i.texto: It shows how the ruler of Jerusalem describes himself to the pharaoh.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-287/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 287 (A Very Grave Crime)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-287/resumen.texto: Letter from Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem, titled «A Very Grave Crime», one of the six written by the scribe of Jerusalem.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-287/por_que_i.texto: It describes an episode in the struggles between Canaanite cities.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-289/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 289 (An Account Is Demanded)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-289/resumen.texto: Letter from Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem, titled «An Account Is Demanded», which names ten people, nine places and the Habiru. It is in the Berlin museum.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-289/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the letters with the most proper names of Canaanite rulers.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-290/resumen.texto: Short letter from Abdi-Heba, titled «Three against One», which sums up the discord between neighbouring cities and their rulers. In the letters from Jerusalem the city is Uru-Salem, «city of peace».

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-290/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the earliest mentions of the name of Jerusalem.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-362/resumen.texto: Letter from Rib-Hadda of Byblos to the pharaoh, titled «A Commissioner Murdered», among the roughly seventy letters of his subcorpus. Byblos was a great port city allied with Egypt, with an Egyptian community.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-362/por_que_i.texto: It shows the insecurity of Egyptian officials on the Lebanese coast.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-366/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 366 (The King of Gath to the Pharaoh)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-366/resumen.texto: Letter from the king of Gath, Shuwardata, to the pharaoh, reporting that he put down a rebellion of the Habiru.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-366/por_que_i.texto: It is evidence of the struggles of Canaanite rulers against the Habiru.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-369/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 369 (From the Pharaoh to Milkilu)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-369/resumen.texto: Letter from the pharaoh to Milkilu of Gezer, one of the few letters in the correspondence written in Egypt and sent to vassals. The tablet is in the Royal Museums of Art and History in Brussels.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-369/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the few surviving letters from the Egyptian side.

fuentes/tablillas-de-taanach/resumen.texto: Thirteen cuneiform tablets (twelve of them in Akkadian) found at Taanach, with the letters exchanged by its king Reshawur with neighbouring kings and with an official who is thought to represent Egypt in Gaza. A third of the names that appear are Hurrian or, broadly, northern.

fuentes/tablillas-de-taanach/por_que_imp.texto: It is the oldest local cuneiform archive of Late Bronze Age Cisjordan, earlier than the Amarna letters.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-34/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 34 (The Pharaoh's Rebuke, Answered)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-34/resumen.texto: Letter from the king of Alashiya to the pharaoh, carefully written on a tablet in very good condition. It answers a rebuke from the pharaoh and includes a list of gifts, with several garments.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-34/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the few written sources on Cyprus in the Late Bronze Age.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-59/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 59 (From the Citizens of Tunip)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-59/resumen.texto: Letter from the city of Tunip to the pharaoh, one of the two Amarna letters that a city sends as such. It deals with the guard of the city, the regional war with the Habiru, and its loyalty and its request for Egyptian protection.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-59/por_que_im.texto: It is the collective voice of a city in northern Syria within the Egyptian correspondence.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-100/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 100 (The City of Irqata to the King)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-100/resumen.texto: Letter from the elders of Irqata (today Arqa, in Lebanon) to the pharaoh, the other letter sent by a city as such. It deals with the guard of the city, the war with the Habiru and its loyalty, and it reveals its need for Egyptian aid.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-100/por_que_i.texto: It shows the situation of a city on the northern Levantine coast facing the Habiru.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-75/resumen.texto: Letter from Rib-Hadda of Byblos to the pharaoh, with some lines missing. It describes the war of the Habiru and the pressure of the great kingdoms of the region (Hatti and Mitanni), with people selling goods in Yarimuta to survive and the countryside left without anyone to work it.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-75/por_que_im.texto: It sums up why Rib-Hadda asked Egypt for help.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-144/resumen.texto: Letter from the ruler of Sidon to the pharaoh, in rough cuneiform writing and almost without gaps. It is one of two letters sent by Zimredda, in the submissive tone of the letters from the cities of Canaan.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-144/por_que_i.texto: It is the voice of Sidon in the Amarna correspondence.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-153/resumen.texto: Short letter from Abimilki of Tyre to the pharaoh, with a special cuneiform sign for «ship». The tablet is preserved in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-153/por_que_i.texto: It shows the role of Tyre, then an island, as a port.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-170/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 170 (To Aziru in Egypt)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-170/resumen.texto: Letter addressed to Aziru when he had already travelled to Egypt, with local news; it reports the capture of the region of Amqu in the war that was still going on in the area. It is the fifteenth of the sixteen letters of the Aziru group.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-170/por_que_i.texto: It places Aziru's stay in Egypt within the war in Syria.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-254/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 254 (Neither Rebel nor Criminal, 2)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-254/resumen.texto: Letter from Labaya of Shechem to the pharaoh, on an intact tablet in the Vorderasiatisches Museum in Berlin. It is the third of the three letters in which Labaya defends himself against accusations of rebellion.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-254/por_que_i.texto: It is the voice of the ruler of Shechem in his dispute with other Canaanite kings.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-299/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 299 (A Request for Help)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-299/resumen.texto: Letter from the governor Yapahu of Gezer to the pharaoh, the third of the four he wrote, with a somewhat eroded surface. The tablet is in the British Museum.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-299/por_que_i.texto: It shows the situation of Gezer in the time of the Amarna letters.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-325/resumen.texto: Letter from Yidya of Ashkelon to the pharaoh, the fifth of the seven surviving from him. He says he is making preparations for the arrival of the Egyptian archers.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-325/por_que_i.texto: It shows how a coastal city prepared for the passage of Egyptian troops.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-330/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 330 (Dust at the King's Feet)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-330/resumen.texto: Short letter from the ruler of Lachish to the pharaoh, with a prostration formula that adds the word «flooding». The tablet is in the British Museum.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-330/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the letters from the city of Lachish in the Amarna period.

fuentes/tratado-de-suppiluliuma-i-con-az.texto: Treaty of Suppiluliuma I with Aziru of Amurru (CTH 49)
Treaty by which Aziru of Amurru became a vassal of the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I, to whom he remained loyal until his death. It is known by its number in the catalogue of Hittite texts, CTH 49.
It documents Amurru's change of allegiance from Egypt to Hatti.

fuentes/archivo-de-la-casa-de-urtenu/tit.texto: Archive of the House of Urtenu

fuentes/archivo-de-la-casa-de-urtenu/aut.texto: Scribes of the house of Urtenu

fuentes/archivo-de-la-casa-de-urtenu/res.texto: Archive of the house of Urtenu, in Ugarit, with documents from the last reigns: Hittite letters about tribute, such as the one from the queen mother Puduheba to Niqmaddu III and the one from Prince Hashshuwash-Inara, and legal texts. A clay tag with the seal of Ammurapi was also found in the house.

fuentes/archivo-de-la-casa-de-urtenu/por.texto: It is a source on the relationship of Ugarit with the Hittites in its final years.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-ramses-iii-en-tay.texto: Hieroglyphic inscription of Ramesses III, found in 2010 about 60 km northwest of Tayma, the first of its kind discovered in Saudi Arabia. It bears the king's name, User-Maat-Ra.
It is evidence of Egyptian presence in northwestern Arabia in the early Iron Age.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-367/titulo.texto: Amarna Letter EA 367 (From the Pharaoh to a Vassal)

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-367/resumen.texto: Letter from the pharaoh to Endaruta of Akshapa, one of about ten letters of the Amarna correspondence that were written by the pharaoh and never received by him. It warns that Hanni is on his way with the army of archers and that he must prepare what he needs.

fuentes/carta-de-amarna-ea-367/por_que_i.texto: It shows how Egypt organized the passage of troops through the cities of Canaan.

fuentes/tratado-de-hattusili-iii-con-ben.texto: Treaty of Hattusili III with Bentesina of Amurru (CTH 92)
Treaty of the Hittite king Hattusili III with Bentesina, whom he restored to the throne of Amurru, binding him as a vassal. It is known by its number in the catalogue of Hittite texts, CTH 92.
It documents Amurru's return to the Hittite orbit after the reign of Shapili.

fuentes/tratado-de-suppiluliuma-i-con-ni.texto: Treaty of Suppiluliuma I with Niqmaddu II of Ugarit (CTH 46 and 47)

Treaty of the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I with Niqmaddu II of Ugarit (CTH 46), and a decree fixing the tribute of Ugarit (CTH 47), together with a letter (CTH 45) and a tribute inventory (CTH 48). They are known by their numbers in the catalogue of Hittite texts.
They document Ugarit's move into the Hittite sphere under Niqmaddu II.

fuentes/estatua-de-ibbit-lim/resumen.texto: Basalt votive statue dedicated to Ishtar, found at Tell Mardikh in 1968, which names Ibbit-Lim as king of Ebla (Mekim) and son of Igrish-Halam. It made it possible to identify the site with ancient Ebla.

fuentes/estatua-de-ibbit-lim/por_que_imp.texto: It is the first document found at the site that identified it with Ebla.

fuentes/jarra-de-laquis/resumen.texto: Canaanite jar of the Late Bronze Age, from the late 13th century BC, found around 1933 in the Fosse Temple III at Lachish by the expedition of James Starkey. A row of animals and trees is accompanied by a proto-Canaanite alphabetic inscription, read as an offering to Asherah.

fuentes/jarra-de-laquis/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the proto-Canaanite inscriptions of the Late Bronze Age and shows Canaanite cult at Lachish.

fuentes/kempinski-tel-kabri-1986-1993/ti.texto: Tel Kabri: las campañas de excavación de 1986-1993

fuentes/kempinski-tel-kabri-1986-1993/au.texto: Aharon Kempinski, N. Scheftelowitz and R. Oren (eds.)

fuentes/kempinski-tel-kabri-1986-1993/so.texto: Book (Emery and Claire Yass Publications in Archaeology)

fuentes/kempinski-tel-kabri-1986-1993/re.texto: Publication of the excavations of Tel Aviv University at Tel Kabri between 1986 and 1993, with the stratigraphy and architecture of the different areas and studies of the frescoes of the Middle Bronze Age palace. The chapters are signed by members of the excavation team.

fuentes/kempinski-tel-kabri-1986-1993/po.texto: It is the publication of the excavation of the Canaanite palace at Kabri and of its Aegean-style frescoes.

fuentes/koh-yasur-landau-cline-bodega-de.texto: Caracterización de una bodega palaciega del Bronce medio en Tel Kabri, Israel
Andrew J. Koh, Assaf Yasur-Landau and Eric H. Cline

Scientific article by the team excavating Tel Kabri on the storeroom of the Middle Bronze Age palace: it describes the room with jars and analyzes with organic chemistry the residues they contained, which indicate wine.
It is the scientific publication of the find of the storeroom, announced in 2013.

fuentes/pfalzner-investigaciones-en-el-p.texto: Investigaciones arqueológicas en el palacio real de Qatna

Report by the director of the German excavations of the royal palace of Tell Mishrifeh, ancient Qatna, on the architecture and phases of the palace. It was published in the proceedings of a conference held in Udine in 2004.
It is a publication of the excavation of the palace, written by the person who directed it.

fuentes/novak-cronologia-del-palacio-rea.texto: La cronología del palacio real de Qatna
Article by the co-director of the project on the sequence of construction and use of the royal palace of Qatna, with its dating based on stratigraphy and the finds.
It fixes the chronology of the palace, which Morandi Bonacossi discussed in a 2007 rebuttal.

fuentes/pfalzner-almaqdissi-estudios-sob.texto: Estudios interdisciplinarios sobre la tumba real de Qatna
First volume of the study series of the German-Syrian Qatna project, on the royal hypogeum found beneath the palace: its architecture, the burials and the finds, in chapters by several specialists.
It is the collective publication of the royal tomb and of the other tombs beneath the palace.

fuentes/greenberg-wengrow-paz-relieve-eg.texto: ¿Conexiones cosméticas? Un relieve egipcio del Bronce antiguo en Tel Bet Yerah
Raphael Greenberg, David Wengrow and Sarit Paz

Note by the excavators on a stone palette with a relief of Egyptian motifs found at Tel Bet Yerah (Khirbet Kerak), with the ankh sign, and on its parallels in Egypt at the beginning of the 3rd millennium BC.
It is the publication of the 2009 find and of what it implies for contacts with Egypt.

fuentes/luck-valle-del-jordan-cuna-de-ci.texto: Newspaper article on what the archaeologist Stephen Bourke, of the University of Sydney, announced about the excavations at Pella, in Jordan: a wall and other structures from around 3400 BC at Tell Husn.
It is the source of the 2010 announcement; it is not a scientific publication.

fuentes/dunand-byblia-grammata/titulo.texto: Byblia Grammata: documentos e investigaciones sobre el desarrollo de la escritura en Fenicia

fuentes/dunand-byblia-grammata/resumen.texto: Study by the excavator of Byblos of the syllabic inscriptions found in the city between 1928 and 1932, and of the origins of writing in Phoenicia.

fuentes/dunand-byblia-grammata/por_que_i.texto: It is the publication of the Byblos syllabary inscriptions by the person who found them.

fuentes/zettler-tell-es-sweyhat-1989-199.texto: Subsistencia y asentamiento en un ambiente marginal: Tell es-Sweyhat, 1989-1995, informe preliminar
Book (MASCA Research Papers in Science and Archaeology 14)

Preliminary report on the campaigns of the University of Pennsylvania at Tell es-Sweyhat, on the Euphrates, between 1989 and 1995: the 3rd-millennium walls, the temple and the tombs found in the mound.
It is the report of the excavation in which the Early Bronze Age cemetery was found.

fuentes/holland-excavaciones-en-tell-es-.texto: Excavaciones en Tell es-Sweyhat, Siria, volumen 2: arqueología de los restos del Bronce, helenísticos y romanos
Publication of the excavations at Tell es-Sweyhat: the architectural remains and the finds of the Bronze Age, including the fortifications.
It is a definitive publication of the site's excavation.

fuentes/van-loon-hammam-et-turkman-1988/.texto: Nuevas pruebas para la cronología del norte de Siria desde Hammam et-Turkman
Article by the director of the University of Amsterdam excavations at Tell Hammam et-Turkman on the site's chronology and its contribution to that of northern Syria.
It is one of the publications on the chronology of Tell Hammam et-Turkman.

fuentes/hameeuw-viviendo-con-los-muertos.texto: Viviendo con los muertos: Tell Tweini, tumbas del Bronce medio en un contexto urbano
Chapter (proceedings of the 5th International Congress on the Archaeology of the Ancient Near East, Madrid 2006, pp. 143-151)
Report by the Syrian-Belgian team at Tell Tweini on the Middle Bronze Age collective tombs found inside the city.
It is the publication of the communal tomb at Tell Tweini.

fuentes/badre-ceramica-brunida-a-mano-de.texto: Cerámica bruñida a mano y cerámica importada contemporánea de Tell Kazel
Chapter (proceedings of the Sea Routes symposium, Rethymno 2002, pp. 83-99)

The director of the excavations of the American University of Beirut at Tell Kazel describes the hand-burnished pottery and the imported pottery of the Late Bronze Age and of the transition to the Iron Age.
It documents the imported and local pottery of the level after the Late Bronze Age destruction.

fuentes/badre-procedencia-de-la-ceramica.texto: La procedencia de la cerámica de tipo egeo y de tipo sirio hallada en Tell Kazel (Siria)
Leila Badre, Marie-Claude Boileau, Reinhard Jung and Hans Mommsen
Analysis of the provenance of the Aegean-type and Syrian-type pottery from Tell Kazel, with the Late Bronze Age and early Iron Age sequence at the site.
It shows which pottery reached Tell Kazel and from where, in the centuries of the Bronze Age transition.

fuentes/briend-humbert-tell-keisan/titul.texto: Tell Keisan (1971-1976): una ciudad fenicia en Galilea

fuentes/briend-humbert-tell-keisan/sopor.texto: Book (Orbis Biblicus et Orientalis, Series Archaeologica 1)

fuentes/briend-humbert-tell-keisan/resum.texto: Publication of the excavations of the French Biblical and Archaeological School at Tell Keisan between 1971 and 1976, with the stratigraphy of the Bronze and Iron Age levels and studies of the materials.

fuentes/briend-humbert-tell-keisan/por_q.texto: It is the publication of the site's excavation.

fuentes/akkermans-schwartz-arqueologia-d.texto: La arqueología de Siria: de los cazadores-recolectores complejos a las sociedades urbanas tempranas (ca. 16 000-300 BC)
Peter M. M. G. Akkermans and Glenn M. Schwartz
Synthesis of the archaeology of Syria up to the end of the 4th century BC, with the Euphrates sites and the interior sites of the Early, Middle and Late Bronze Age.
It is a general reference on the Syrian Bronze Age sites.

fuentes/wilkinson-al-margen-del-eufrates.texto: Al margen del Éufrates: asentamiento y uso de la tierra en Tell es-Sweyhat y en la región alta del lago Assad
Study of settlement and land use in the region of Tell es-Sweyhat and the upper Lake Assad, with the Syrian Euphrates sites rescued before the flooding, including Tell Fray.
It places Tell Fray and Tell es-Sweyhat in the settlement of the Syrian Euphrates.

fuentes/schwartz-umm-el-marra-1996-1997/.texto: Excavación y prospección en la llanura de Jabbul, Siria occidental: el proyecto Umm el-Marra, 1996-1997
Report on the 1996 and 1997 campaigns of Johns Hopkins University at Umm el-Marra and on the survey of the Jabbul plain, with the site's sequence.
It is the scientific report on the site's excavations.

personas/igrish-halam/resumen.texto: King of Ebla of the first kingdom, active around 2360 BC. His name means «the god of Halab has driven out the opponent», and it is read as a memory of an Eblaite victory that added lands beyond Aleppo.

personas/irkab-damu/resumen.texto: King (malikum) of the first kingdom of Ebla, whose reign ended around 2340 BC; under him Ebla became the dominant power in the Levant. He appointed the first vizier, Arrukum, and during his reign a treaty was concluded with Enna-Dagan of Mari. His reign stands out for Ebla's wide diplomatic relations.

personas/isar-damu/resumen.texto: King (malikum) of the first kingdom of Ebla, who died around 2305 BC after a reign of about 35 years. He waged a long war against Mari that ended in an Eblaite victory; he was probably the last king of that kingdom, which fell shortly afterwards with the fire of Palace G.

personas/arrukum/resumen.texto: First vizier of Ebla, appointed by King Irkab-Damu (around 2350 BC). He is known from the texts of the archive of Palace G, not from inscriptions of his own, and was in charge of administration and the army. Without an article of his own, he is described in the article on the viziers of Ebla.

personas/ibrium/resumen.texto: Vizier of Ebla under Irkab-Damu and under Isar-Damu, who died around 2322 BC. The texts show him on campaign almost every year, including against Abarsal and Armi, and his son Ibbi-Sipish succeeded him, so the office became hereditary.

personas/ibbi-sipish/resumen.texto: Vizier of Ebla for 17 years under Isar-Damu, son of Ibrium; he died around 2300 BC. The texts show him on missions abroad, including in Kish, and concluding a treaty with Armi; they also record the defeat of King Hida'ar of Mari.

personas/ibbit-lim/resumen.texto: Earliest known ruler of the third kingdom of Ebla, active around 1975 BC (middle chronology); he is named as the first king of that series.

personas/immeya/resumen.texto: King of Ebla of the third kingdom, who ruled around 1750-1725 BC in the Middle Bronze Age IIA, with Ebla subject to the kingdom of Yamhad.

personas/sumu-epuh/resumen.texto: First attested king of Yamhad (Halab), founder of the dynasty that dominated northern Syria in the 18th and 17th centuries BC. He fought Yahdun-Lim of Mari and Shamshi-Adad I and, according to the scholarship, died in one of those struggles around 1780 BC.

personas/hammurabi-i-de-yamhad/resumen.texto: Third attested king of Yamhad, son of Yarim-Lim I, who died around 1750 BC. Under his reign the kingdom kept its hegemony and added Karkemish to its vassals.

personas/abba-el-i/resumen.texto: Fourth great king of Yamhad, son of Hammurabi I, who died around 1720 BC. He destroyed Irridu, which had rebelled, and gave Alalakh to his brother Yarim-Lim, who founded a minor branch of the dynasty there.

personas/yarim-lim-ii/resumen.texto: King of Yamhad, who died around 1700 BC; his reign is poorly documented, and on a seal he declares himself son of Abba-El I.

personas/niqmi-epuh/resumen.texto: King of Yamhad, son of Yarim-Lim II, who died around 1675 BC; with his successor Irkabtum he fought the Hurrian principalities of the north.

personas/irkabtum/resumen.texto: King of Yamhad, son of Niqmi-Epuh, who died around 1658 BC.

personas/hammurabi-ii-de-yamhad/resumen.texto: Little-known king of Yamhad, who is thought to have reigned after Irkabtum, in the mid-17th century BC.

personas/yarim-lim-iii/resumen.texto: King of Yamhad who succeeded Hammurabi II and reigned until around 1625 BC (middle chronology). According to the scholarship, he defeated Qatna, the dynasty's old rival.

personas/hammurabi-iii-de-yamhad/resumen.texto: King of Yamhad who reigned around 1625-1600 BC (middle chronology) and succeeded Yarim-Lim III; his reign coincides with the Hittite campaigns against Aleppo.

personas/sarra-el/resumen.texto: King of Yamhad who, according to the scholarship, regained the throne after the assassination of the Hittite Mursili I; he died around 1575 BC.

personas/abba-el-ii/resumen.texto: King of Yamhad who reigned after the withdrawal of the Hittites; he died around 1550 BC and is known from his seal.

personas/ilim-ilimma-i/resumen.texto: Last king of Yamhad to rule Aleppo, who died around 1524 BC. A rebellion, probably instigated by Parshatatar of Mitanni, ended his reign and his life around 1524 BC; the statue of his son Idrimi says that the family fled to Emar.

personas/ammitakum/resumen.texto: King of Alalakh around 1700 BC, vassal of the kingdom of Yamhad, of the minor branch founded by Yarim-Lim; he claimed a certain autonomy without declaring himself independent.

personas/idrimi/resumen.texto: King of Alalakh around 1490-1465 BC or around 1450 BC, son of Ilim-Ilimma I of Yamhad. According to the inscription on his statue, he lived seven years among the Habiru, landed in Mukish, and Barattarna of Mitanni (Parshatatar for many scholars) recognized him as king of Alalakh, with Mukish as a vassal kingdom.

personas/niqmepa-de-mukish/resumen.texto: King of Mukish, with capital at Alalakh, in the mid or late 15th century BC, son of Idrimi.

personas/ishi-addu/resumen.texto: King of Qatna in the first half of the 18th century BC, died around 1772 BC. His letters with Shamshi-Adad I, his closest ally, show him in constant war with Yamhad and with revolts in the south of his kingdom.

personas/amut-pi-el-ii/resumen.texto: King of Qatna in the 18th century BC, died around 1750 BC and successor of Ishi-Addu.

personas/idanda/resumen.texto: King of Qatna in the mid-14th century BC, known from the archive of tablets of the royal palace, where he is called the son of a king Ulasuda. He was a vassal of the Hittites of Suppiluliuma I, although the chronology of Qatna's submission is debated.

personas/ammittamru-i/resumen.texto: King of Ugarit around the mid-14th century BC, died around 1350 BC. A letter from him (EA 45), probably to Amenhotep III, shows cordial relations with Egypt.

personas/niqmaddu-ii/resumen.texto: King of Ugarit around 1350-1315 BC, son of Ammittamru I. He became a vassal of the Hittite Suppiluliuma I; he also kept up correspondence with Egypt, as the Amarna letters show.

personas/arhalba/resumen.texto: King of Ugarit between Niqmaddu II and Niqmepa, known from the royal list of Ugarit and from texts in the archive.

personas/niqmepa-de-ugarit/resumen.texto: King of Ugarit, father of Ammittamru II, died around 1270 BC. He signed a treaty of vassalage with the Hittites.

personas/ammittamru-ii/resumen.texto: King of Ugarit between 1260 and 1235 BC, son of Niqmepa, who had signed the treaty of vassalage with the Hittites.

personas/ibiranu/resumen.texto: Sixth king of Ugarit, who reigned around 1235-1225 BC.

personas/niqmaddu-iii/resumen.texto: Seventh known king of Ugarit, who reigned between 1225 and 1220 BC and succeeded Ibiranu.

personas/ammurapi/resumen.texto: Last king of Ugarit (c. 1215-1185 BC), contemporary of the Hittite Suppiluliuma II. His letters describe the enemy ships that burned his cities while his army and fleet were away; the kingdom fell shortly afterwards.

personas/du-tessub-de-amurru/resumen.texto: Ruler of Amurru around 1310 BC, vassal of the Hittite Mursili II, son of Aziru and father of Duppi-Teššup.

personas/ili-rapih/resumen.texto: Brother of Rib-Hadda of Byblos who, according to the Amarna letters, overthrew him in a palace coup while he was away in Beirut; he is the author of two Amarna letters (EA 139 and 140).

personas/ammunira/resumen.texto: King of Biruta (Beirut) around 1350 BC, author of the Amarna letters EA 141-143; at one point Rib-Hadda took refuge under his protection.

personas/zimredda-de-sidon/resumen.texto: Only king of Sidon in the Amarna correspondence (c. 1350-1335 BC), author of letters EA 144-145; he is the subject of many letters from Abimilki of Tyre and from Rib-Hadda.

personas/mutbaal/resumen.texto: Canaanite ruler of Pella, east of the Jordan, son of Labaya of Shechem. After his father's death he continued, together with his brother, the attacks on other Canaanite kings with the help of the Habiru.

personas/adda-danu/resumen.texto: Ruler of Gezer in the Amarna period, author of letter EA 292.

personas/yapahu/resumen.texto: Ruler of Gezer around 1340 BC, author of five Amarna letters (EA 297-300 and EA 378).

personas/suwardata/resumen.texto: Ruler of Gat (Tell es-Safi), according to most scholars, or of Qiltu, in the Amarna letters; he wrote eight letters to the pharaoh.

personas/yidya/resumen.texto: Canaanite king of Ashkelon in the Amarna correspondence (c. 1350-1335 BC), author of letters EA 320-326; there is also a letter from the pharaoh addressed to him (EA 370).

personas/zimredda-de-laquis/resumen.texto: Ruler of Lachish around 1340 BC, author of letter EA 329; Abdi-Heba reports in EA 288 that he died at the hands of the Habiru.

personas/biryawaza/resumen.texto: Ruler of the Damascus region and of the Beqaa around 1350 BC, known from the Amarna letters; some consider him king of Damascus and others a senior Egyptian official.

personas/etakkama/resumen.texto: Ruler of Qadesh (Qidshu) in the Amarna letters (c. 1350-1335 BC), mentioned in eleven letters and author of several of them concerning the Beqaa region.

personas/pawura/resumen.texto: Egyptian official of the Amarna period, called commander of archers, who acted in the Levantine region; he is named in the letters of Rib-Hadda of Byblos, of Aziru and of Abdi-Heba, and Rib-Hadda's letter EA 362 tells of his death. The place given is that of the sender, not of his seat.

personas/yabitiri/resumen.texto: Ruler of an unknown city in southern Canaan, near Gaza and Jaffa (the place is only an approximate reference), author of the Amarna letter EA 296.

personas/kun-damu/resumen.texto: King (malikum) of the first kingdom of Ebla, active around 2400 BC and known from archive texts written two generations after his reign. According to Alfonso Archi he was a contemporary of Sa'umu of Mari, and he has been proposed as the Eblaite king who defeated Mari in the 25th century BC; he was deified, and his cult is attested at Ebla at least thirty years after his death.

personas/yarim-lim-de-alalakh/resumen.texto: King of Alalakh, son of Hammurabi I of Yamhad, died around 1700 BC. His brother Abba-El I of Yamhad handed Alalakh over to him, and with him began a minor branch of the Yamhad dynasty, which lasted until the city was conquered by the Hittite Hattusili I.

personas/ahatmilku/resumen.texto: Princess of Amurru, daughter of DU-Teššup and sister of Duppi-Teššup, who married King Niqmepa of Ugarit; she had great wealth and influence. According to the scholarship, she supported the succession of her son Ammittamru II and, when two of her sons disputed it, she exiled them to Alashiya with sufficient provisions.

personas/pu-balu-de-yursa/resumen.texto: Ruler of Yursa, a Canaanite city-state identified with Tell Jemmeh, at the time of the Amarna letters (c. 1350-1335 BC). He wrote three letters to the pharaoh Akhenaten (EA 314-316).

personas/yanhamu/resumen.texto: Egyptian commissioner mentioned in the Amarna correspondence (c. 1350-1335 BC), who acted in Canaan as the pharaoh's representative.

personas/reanap/resumen.texto: Egyptian commissioner of the time of the Amarna letters (c. 1350-1335 BC), mentioned in three of them: EA 292, EA 315 and EA 326.

personas/tahmassi/resumen.texto: Egyptian official of the time of the Amarna letters (c. 1350 BC), who appears in four of them (EA 265, 303, 316 and 364). His name is the Akkadian form of the Egyptian Ptah-mes, «born of Ptah».

personas/pihuri/resumen.texto: Egyptian commissioner in the «land of Retenu» (Canaan), who probably served under Amenhotep III or Akhenaten. In letter EA 122 Rib-Hadda of Byblos complains that he attacked, killed Shardana mercenaries of Byblos and captured three of his men.

personas/ayyab/resumen.texto: Possible ruler of Astartu (Tell Ashtara, south of Damascus) around 1350 BC, at the time of the Amarna letters, which tell of Habiru attacks on the cities of the region. The letters do not clearly indicate his title.

personas/endaruta/resumen.texto: Ruler of Akshapa (Achshaph) around 1340 BC, at the time of the Amarna letters. He is the author of letter EA 223 and the addressee of EA 367, from the pharaoh, who orders him to guard his city and prepare what is needed for the passage of the army of archers.

personas/arsawuya/resumen.texto: Possible mayor of Ruhizzi, east of Qadesh and beyond the Anti-Lebanon, around 1340 BC. He appears in five Amarna letters, two of them written by him to the pharaoh (EA 191 and 192).

personas/bentesina/resumen.texto: Ruler of Amurru (Akkar plain) in a first reign until c. 1274 BC, when Muwatalli II deposed him for having gone over to the Egyptians and put Shapili in his place, and in a second reign from c. 1260 to c. 1235 BC, restored by Hattusili III; he was a vassal of both him and Tudhaliya IV. Son and successor of Duppi-Teššup, his daughter married Ammittamru II of Ugarit, and he was succeeded by his son Šaušgamuwa.

personas/indilimma/resumen.texto: Probably the last king of Ebla, active around 1600 BC. He is known from a seal of his crown prince Maratewari, and the city was destroyed shortly afterwards by Mursili I.

personas/duppi-tessub-de-amurru/resumen.texto: Ruler of Amurru, in the Akkar plain, around 1310-1300 BC, during the reign of the Hittite Mursili II. He was father of Bentesina and of Ahatmilku, the wife of Niqmepa of Ugarit, according to his son and his sister.

personas/adad-nirari-de-nuhasse/resumen.texto: King of Nuhašše, southeast of Aleppo and north of Qatna, in the 14th century BC, died around 1345 BC. Formerly part of Mitanni, he fought the Hittites and asked Egypt for help; he formed a coalition that invaded Ugarit, already a Hittite vassal, and that led Suppiluliuma I to intervene. His fate is unknown: he disappears from the records.

personas/abdi-risa/resumen.texto: Ruler of Enišasi in the time of the Amarna letters (c. 1350-1335 BC), known only from his letter EA 363 to the pharaoh, which forms a series with EA 174-176 on the region of Amqu, the Beqaa.

hechos/primer-reino-de-ebla/titulo.texto: First Kingdom of Ebla and Its Archive

hechos/primer-reino-de-ebla/resumen.texto: At the time of the archive of Palace G, around 2400-2300 BC, Ebla was the dominant power among the city-states of northern Syria, with a wide diplomatic network and wars with Mari.

hechos/arrukum-primer-visir-de-ebla/resu.texto: With King Irkab-Damu the vizier appears in Ebla, the head of the administration and the army and second in rank in the kingdom; Arrukum is the first, around 2350 BC. The texts know him through the administration of Ebla; the title «vizier» is a term of modern scholars.

hechos/tratado-de-ebla-y-abarsal-hecho/r.texto: Around 2350 BC Ebla and the city of Abarsal, whose location is unknown, signed a treaty that may be the oldest recorded diplomatic treaty in history.

hechos/campana-de-ibrium-contra-abarsal/.texto: Campaign of the Vizier Ibrium against Abarsal
The texts of Ebla show the vizier Ibrium on campaign against the city of Abarsal, while Arrukum was still vizier; Ibrium held office for nearly two decades, almost always at war.

hechos/guerra-de-ebla-y-mari/resumen.texto: Ebla and Mari were at war for decades; Mari defeated Nagar, an ally of Ebla, and blocked its trade routes to southern Mesopotamia. According to scholars, Ibbi-Sipish defeated King Hida'ar of Mari in year 32 of Isar-Damu, and the destruction of Ebla came a few years later.

hechos/visirato-hereditario-de-ebla/titu.texto: The Vizierate of Ebla Becomes Hereditary

hechos/visirato-hereditario-de-ebla/resu.texto: With King Isar-Damu the office of vizier became hereditary: Ibbi-Sipish succeeded his father Ibrium and formed a dynasty of viziers parallel to the royal one.

hechos/primera-destruccion-de-ebla/resum.texto: Around 2300 BC a fire destroyed Palace G and baked the tablets of the archive. It is attributed to Mari (Alfonso Archi, Mario Liverani), to Sargon or Naram-Sin of Akkad (Paolo Matthiae; Michael Astour rejects this) or to a natural catastrophe (Astour); Pettinato proposed an earlier date, c. 2500-2400 BC.

hechos/segundo-reino-de-ebla/resumen.texto: After the destruction of Palace G the city continued under a new local dynasty, with continuity with the first kingdom; a palace was built in the lower city. Its end, by fire, came towards the end of the 21st century BC.

hechos/segunda-destruccion-de-ebla/resum.texto: The second kingdom ended with the destruction of the city by fire at some point between 2050 and 1950 BC; 2000 BC is a conventional date. It is debated whether a Hurrian invasion caused it.

hechos/tercer-reino-de-ebla/titulo.texto: Third Kingdom of Ebla, a Planned City of the Middle Bronze Age

hechos/tercer-reino-de-ebla/resumen.texto: In the Middle Bronze Age Ebla was rebuilt as a planned city with palaces, temples and two circuits of walls, one for the lower city and another for the acropolis. In the Middle Bronze Age IIA it was a vassal of Yamhad.

hechos/destruccion-de-ebla-por-mursili-i.texto: Destruction of Ebla by Mursili I

Around 1600 BC the Hittite king Mursili I destroyed Ebla in his campaigns against Yamhad; the city never recovered and was a small village in the following centuries. Indilimma may have been its last king, according to a seal of his crown prince Maratewari.

hechos/descubrimiento-del-archivo-de-ebl.texto: In 1974-1975 Paolo Matthiae and his team found the tablets of the archive in Palace G at Tell Mardikh, in situ on collapsed shelves.

hechos/fundacion-de-yamhad/titulo.texto: Sumu-Epuh Founds the Kingdom of Yamhad

hechos/fundacion-de-yamhad/resumen.texto: At the end of the 19th century BC Sumu-Epuh founded the Yamhad dynasty with its capital at Aleppo. He appears in history as an enemy in the inscriptions of Yahdun-Lim of Mari, and he died fighting Shamshi-Adad I.

hechos/yamhad-gran-reino/titulo.texto: Yarim-Lim I and the Great Kingdom of Yamhad

hechos/yamhad-gran-reino/resumen.texto: Yarim-Lim I defeated the enemies of his father and made Yamhad a great kingdom again, which dominated northern Syria; the texts of Mari show him as an ally of Zimri-Lim and his father-in-law.

hechos/yamhad-suma-karkemish/titulo.texto: Yamhad Adds Karkemish to Its Vassals

hechos/yamhad-suma-karkemish/resumen.texto: Under Hammurabi I, son of Yarim-Lim I, the kingdom kept its hegemony and added Karkemish to its vassals.

hechos/yarim-lim-de-alalakh/titulo.texto: Yarim-Lim Receives Alalakh from His Brother Abba-El I

hechos/yarim-lim-de-alalakh/resumen.texto: Abba-El I of Aleppo had destroyed Irridu, which had rebelled, and gave Alalakh to his brother Yarim-Lim, who founded a minor branch of the Yamhad dynasty that reigned there until the mid-17th century BC.

hechos/hattusili-i-ataca-yamhad/titulo.texto: Hattusili I Attacks Yamhad and Destroys Alalakh VII

hechos/hattusili-i-ataca-yamhad/resumen.texto: Around 1630-1620 BC the Hittite Hattusili I (c. 1650-1620 BC, middle chronology) attacked Yamhad and subjected Alalakh, whose stratum VII was destroyed by fire: recent excavations place this around 1650 BC, and the Hittite chronology places it in the 1620s. Mursili I (c. 1620-1590 BC) continued with new raids around 1600-1590 BC, which caused the collapse of the great kingdom.

hechos/mursili-i-toma-alepo/resumen.texto: At the beginning of the 16th century BC the Hittite Mursili I expelled the dynasty of Yamhad from Aleppo in a brief occupation; Sarra-El may have recovered Aleppo after the assassination of Mursili I (c. 1620-1590 BC).

hechos/caida-de-alepo-ante-mitani/resume.texto: Around 1524 BC a rebellion, probably instigated by Parshatatar of Mitanni, ended the reign and life of Ilim-Ilimma I, and Aleppo passed into the orbit of Mitanni, ending the kingdom of Yamhad. The statue of Idrimi says only that in Aleppo «something bad happened» and tells of the flight of the royal family to Emar.

hechos/idrimi-toma-alalakh/titulo.texto: Idrimi Is Recognized as King of Alalakh and Mukish

hechos/idrimi-toma-alalakh/resumen.texto: According to his statue, Idrimi, son of the king of Aleppo, lived seven years among the Habiru, landed in Mukish with ships and auxiliary troops, and Barattarna of Mitanni recognized him as king of Alalakh as a vassal, with Mukish as an allied kingdom. The article also notes that some scholars consider it probable that he won the throne with the help of the Habiru; the inscription does not say so.

hechos/suplicas-de-qatna/titulo.texto: Akizzi Asks Egypt for Help against the Invaders

hechos/suplicas-de-qatna/resumen.texto: Akizzi of Qatna wrote to the pharaoh asking for help against invaders, in the context of the Hittite advance into Syria; his letters were found at Amarna.

hechos/conquista-hitita-de-siria-occiden.texto: Suppiluliuma I Conquers the Kingdoms West of the Euphrates

Around 1345 BC, from the Syrian side, the kingdoms west of the Euphrates that recognized Mitanni (Aleppo, Mukish with Alalakh, Niya, Qatna and Nuhasse) were subjected to Suppiluliuma I (c. 1350-1322 BC) after his crossing of the Euphrates. Karkemish remained under Mitanni until its later siege.

hechos/destruccion-de-qatna/titulo.texto: Destruction of the Royal Palace of Qatna

hechos/destruccion-de-qatna/resumen.texto: The royal palace of Qatna was destroyed by fire around 1340 BC; for Jacques Freu it was the work of the Mitanni king Tushratta, who had invaded Qatna after Idanda passed to the Hittites, while for Gernot Wilhelm the submission to the Hittites came later. The treaty of Shattiwaza says that Qatna was invaded and destroyed and its people deported; Akizzi still reigned afterwards, so Suppiluliuma I's final sack came after the palace fire and before the death of Akhenaten (c. 1334 BC).

hechos/suppiluliuma-i-toma-qadesh/titulo.texto: Suppiluliuma I Defeats Shutatarra of Qadesh

hechos/suppiluliuma-i-toma-qadesh/resume.texto: Suppiluliuma I wanted to avoid Qadesh, a dependency of Egypt, but its king Shutatarra provoked him; the Hittites won and took the king and his family into captivity. They then allowed the son, Aitakkama, to return as a vassal.

hechos/emar-bajo-los-hititas/titulo.texto: Emar Passes to the Hittite Sphere

hechos/emar-bajo-los-hititas/resumen.texto: After the defeat of Tushratta of Mitanni by Suppiluliuma I around 1345 BC, Emar passed to the Hittite Empire as the capital of the province of Astata, under the viceroyalty of Karkemish.

hechos/caida-de-emar/resumen.texto: The written and archaeological record of Emar ends at the end of the 12th century BC; the destruction of the city is dated to 1187 BC, in the second year of Meli-Shipak II of Babylon, in the context of the collapse at the end of the Bronze Age.

hechos/destruccion-de-tell-fray/resumen.texto: The site was destroyed by fire in the 13th century BC, probably by the Middle Assyrian kings Shalmaneser I or Tukulti-Ninurta I when they conquered the area.

hechos/destruccion-de-umm-el-marra/resum.texto: The city passed to the Hittite Empire after the fall of Karkemish and the death of Tushratta around 1345 BC, and it was destroyed in the 14th century BC.

hechos/palacio-real-de-qatna-hecho/resum.texto: Kings Ishi-Addu and Amut-pi-El had the royal palace built; it was completed between 1790 and 1760 BC and was the largest in the Levant of its time, with 16 000 m² and at least eighty rooms on the upper floor.

hechos/tumba-real-de-qatna/titulo.texto: Discovery of the Royal Tomb of Qatna

hechos/tumba-real-de-qatna/resumen.texto: Since 2002 a German-Syrian team led by Peter Pfälzner has excavated the royal hypogeum, 12 metres below the palace, with four chambers cut into the rock and a corridor 40 m long, as well as other tombs beneath the palace.

hechos/ishi-addu-aliado-de-shamshi-adad/.texto: Ishi-Addu of Qatna, Ally of Shamshi-Adad I
The texts of Mari show Ishi-Addu of Qatna as the closest ally of Shamshi-Adad I, while Qatna fought Yamhad and faced revolts in the south.

hechos/alfabeto-ugaritico/resumen.texto: Around 1400 BC the scribes of Ugarit used a consonantal alphabet of 30 signs, made with a stylus on clay, to write Ugaritic; it is the oldest alphabet in systematic use, and it went out of use around 1190 BC.

hechos/hallazgo-de-ugarit/titulo.texto: Discovery of Ugarit at Ras Shamra

hechos/hallazgo-de-ugarit/resumen.texto: In 1928-1929 several deposits of clay tablets, written in an unknown language, were found by chance at Ras Shamra; in the following campaigns, between 1929 and 1937, the acropolis with the temples of Dagan and Baal was excavated and the royal area was found.

hechos/ammittamru-i-escribe-a-egipto/tit.texto: Ammittamru I of Ugarit Writes to Egypt

hechos/ammittamru-i-escribe-a-egipto/res.texto: A letter from Ammittamru I (EA 45), probably to Amenhotep III, shows cordial relations with Egypt.

hechos/ugarit-vasalla-de-hatti/titulo.texto: Ugarit Becomes a Vassal of the Hittites

hechos/ugarit-vasalla-de-hatti/resumen.texto: Under Niqmaddu II (c. 1350-1315 BC) Ugarit became a vassal of the Hittite Empire of Suppiluliuma I, which fixed the relationship in a treaty (CTH 46) and in a tribute decree (CTH 47). The kingdom kept diplomatic relations with Egypt, as a letter from Niqmaddu II shows (EA 49), and Niqmaddu II commissioned the Baal cycle.

hechos/tratado-de-niqmepa-con-hatti/titu.texto: Niqmepa's Treaty of Vassalage with the Hittites

hechos/tratado-de-niqmepa-con-hatti/resu.texto: The Hittite king Mursili II (c. 1321-1300 BC) forced Arhalba to abdicate, put his brother Niqmepa on the throne of Ugarit, and imposed a treaty declaring Ugarit a vassal of the Hittites (the text CTH 66, found at Ugarit). The date within the reign of Mursili II is approximate.

hechos/cartas-de-ugarit-a-egipto/titulo.texto: Ugarit Asks for a Statue of Merneptah

hechos/cartas-de-ugarit-a-egipto/resumen.texto: In the time of Merneptah a king of Ugarit, perhaps Ammurapi or his predecessor Niqmaddu III, asked for a sculptor to make an image of the pharaoh before the statue of Baal in his temple; the pharaoh delayed or refused and sent gifts.

hechos/hambruna-en-ugarit/titulo.texto: Famine in Ugarit and Requests for Grain

hechos/hambruna-en-ugarit/resumen.texto: From the late 13th century BC the eastern Mediterranean suffered famines; Ugarit, a great supplier of food, received desperate requests for grain from other states, and in turn asked for help: a letter from Ammurapi says there is severe famine and asks the king for wheat.

hechos/ataque-naval-a-ugarit/titulo.texto: Enemy Ships Burn the Cities of Ugarit

hechos/ataque-naval-a-ugarit/resumen.texto: Ammurapi confirmed to the king of Alashiya, who had warned him of enemy ships, that they arrived and burned his cities while his troops and chariots were in Hatti and his ships in Lukka. In another letter, to the Hittite viceroy of Karkemish, he reports that the enemy is at Ra'šu and that its vanguard was sent to Ugarit.

hechos/destruccion-de-ugarit/resumen.texto: Around 1185 BC (other dates, 1192-1190 BC; a letter between the chancellor Bay, an official of Queen Tausert, and Ammurapi fixes 1194 BC as the earliest possible date), Ugarit was set on fire and sacked, and the Hittite reinforcements sent from Karkemish arrived when it had already been razed. Scholars debate who the attackers were; a later letter says the city was looted and the grain burned.

hechos/destruccion-final-de-alalakh/resu.texto: The first palace, from c. 2000 BC, was probably destroyed in the 12th century BC; Eric Cline argues that the city was almost abandoned around 1300 BC, with a small Hittite post. There was occupation in the Iron Age.

hechos/rib-hadda-pide-ayuda/titulo.texto: Rib-Hadda of Byblos Asks for Help against Abdi-Ashirta

hechos/rib-hadda-pide-ayuda/resumen.texto: In some sixty letters to the pharaoh, Rib-Hadda asks for military help against Abdi-Ashirta, who is taking coastal cities; in EA 105 he asks for intervention over a conflict with Beirut.

hechos/muerte-de-abdi-ashirta/titulo.texto: Capture of Abdi-Ashirta by the Egyptians

hechos/muerte-de-abdi-ashirta/resumen.texto: Abdi-Ashirta of Amurru, who raided his neighbors with the help of habiru groups, was captured in a late Egyptian military action; his son Aziru renewed the attacks.

hechos/exilio-de-rib-hadda/resumen.texto: At one point Rib-Hadda had to flee from Byblos into exile in Beirut, under the protection of King Ammunira.

hechos/aziru-de-amurru-y-los-hititas/tit.texto: Aziru of Amurru moves from Egypt to Hatti

hechos/aziru-de-amurru-y-los-hititas/res.texto: Aziru, son of Abdi-Ashirta, kept expanding Amurru against Egypt's vassals and eventually passed into the Hittite orbit of Suppiluliuma I; his descendants signed treaties with Hatti.

hechos/cartas-de-abdi-heba-hecho/titulo.texto: Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem asks Egypt for help

hechos/cartas-de-abdi-heba-hecho/resumen.texto: From Jerusalem, Abdi-Heba wrote six letters to the pharaoh denouncing attacks by the habiru and other rulers and asking for troops or an Egyptian commissioner.

hechos/muerte-de-zimredda-de-laquis/titu.texto: Zimredda of Lachish dies at the hands of the habiru

hechos/muerte-de-zimredda-de-laquis/resu.texto: Abdi-Heba informs the pharaoh in letter EA 288 that Zimredda, ruler of Lachish, was killed by the habiru.

hechos/labayu-de-siquem/titulo.texto: Labayu of Shechem and the Canaanite cities

hechos/labayu-de-siquem/resumen.texto: Labayu, ruler of Shechem, gave land to the habiru, clashed with other Canaanite kings, and defended himself against charges of rebellion before the pharaoh; he died at the hands of the people of Gina, and his sons continued the attacks.

hechos/cartas-de-amarna-de-gezer/titulo.texto: The rulers of Gezer in the Amarna letters

hechos/cartas-de-amarna-de-gezer/resumen.texto: Three rulers of Gezer, Milkilu, Yapahu and Adda-danu, wrote to the pharaoh; Milkilu, son-in-law of Tagi, was accused of allying with Labayu and of hiring habiru mercenaries.

hechos/cartas-de-abimilki-de-tiro-hecho/.texto: Abimilki of Tyre reports on Sidon and Amurru
Abimilki, confirmed on the throne of Tyre by the pharaoh, wrote ten letters, half of them about the intrigues of Zimredda of Sidon and of Aziru.

hechos/alashiya-envia-cobre-a-egipto/res.texto: In the Amarna letters the king of Alashiya deals with the pharaoh over Cypriot copper, for which he receives silver and ivory in return, and he apologizes for sending less than he had promised (500 talents). The capital of Alashiya has not been identified with certainty; Enkomi is one of the candidates.

hechos/los-habiru-en-las-cartas-de-amarn.texto: The habiru in the Amarna letters

Regional phenomenon not located at Jerusalem, reference point. The Amarna letters and other texts of the second millennium BC name the ʿapiru (habiru) as a social group of rebels, mercenaries, slaves or day laborers. Some early scholars identified them with the Hebrews because of the similarity of the names, but most current scholars reject that idea, though they accept that some Israelites may have come from that class.

hechos/los-shasu-en-las-fuentes-egipcias.texto: Regional phenomenon not located at Gaza, reference point. The shasu were nomadic herders of the southern Levant who spoke a Semitic language, from the Late Bronze Age to the early Iron Age; they were described as bandits active from the Jezreel Valley to Ashkelon, in Transjordan and in Sinai, and some of them were mercenaries. The connection with the early Israelites is debated.

hechos/hazor-en-los-textos-de-mari/resum.texto: The Mari texts from the reigns of Yasmah-Adad and Zimri-Lim mention Hazor, its king Ibni-Addu (c. 1770-1765 BC), and the trade route Hazor-Qatna-Mari, by which Mari received tin.

hechos/hazor-juramento-a-egipto/titulo.texto: Abdi-Tirshi of Hazor swears loyalty to Egypt

hechos/hazor-juramento-a-egipto/resumen.texto: In the Amarna period Abdi-Tirshi, king of Hazor, swore loyalty to the pharaoh, while Abimilki of Tyre accused Hazor of having gone over to the habiru (EA 148).

hechos/destruccion-de-hazor-bronce-tardi.texto: Destruction of Hazor in the Late Bronze Age

In the 13th century BC a palace at Hazor was burned, with signs of violent destruction. Amnon Ben-Tor sees it as confirmation of the biblical account, Sharon Zuckerman attributes it to a conflict between factions within the city itself, and Norman Gottwald to a group later identified with the tribe of Naphtali.

hechos/puerta-de-tel-dan/titulo.texto: Gate of Tel Dan with mudbrick arches

hechos/puerta-de-tel-dan/resumen.texto: The city gate, made of mudbrick on basalt orthostats, was built around 1750 BC, and its three arches are among the oldest complete monumental arches.

hechos/palacio-de-tel-kabri/resumen.texto: In the Middle Bronze Age, Tel Kabri had one of the largest Canaanite palaces, the largest excavated up to 2014, with frescoes in Minoan style. In its cellar, announced in 2013, 40 large jars (about 2000 liters) with wine residue from c. 1700 BC were found; it is the oldest palatial wine cellar known in the Near East.

hechos/siquem-en-el-bronce-medio/resumen.texto: Around 1900 BC, in the Middle Bronze IIA, Shechem had its first major building project and became a very large Canaanite settlement, attacked by Egypt according to the stela of Sebek-khu.

hechos/jerico-en-el-bronce-antiguo/titul.texto: Jericho in the Early Bronze Age

hechos/jerico-en-el-bronce-antiguo/resum.texto: The city of Tell es-Sultan reached its greatest extent in the Early Bronze Age around 2600 BC; in EB IIIB there was a palace on the spring hill and city walls.

hechos/destruccion-de-bab-edh-dhra/resum.texto: Bab edh-Dhra was abandoned around 2350 BC, after a cemetery in use since Early Bronze IA had accumulated some 20,000 tombs. Some proposed it as the biblical Sodom, but its date, size and location do not match the tradition.

hechos/destruccion-de-numeira/resumen.texto: The site was violently destroyed at the end of Early Bronze III, c. 2300 BC (or 2100-2050 BC according to another proposal), and was never reoccupied.

hechos/colapso-urbano-del-bronce-antiguo.texto: Urban collapse in Early Bronze IV

In the Levant, the cities of Early Bronze III lost their central authority at the end of the third millennium BC; on the Jabbul Plain between 2200 and 2000 BC, with a dry climate, although Umm el-Marra was not completely abandoned. It coincides with the climate event of c. 2200 BC noted in other packages. Causes are debated: drought according to some, other political reasons according to others.

hechos/arad-ciudad-fortificada/titulo.texto: Arad, large fortified city of Early Bronze II

hechos/arad-ciudad-fortificada/resumen.texto: Around 3050-2750 BC Arad was a large fortified city with rich remains; in EB IB, imports of Egyptian pottery were found, showing trade with Egypt.

hechos/pella-ciudad-amurallada/resumen.texto: In 2010 the discovery at Tell Husn of a wall and other structures from around 3400 BC was announced, which indicate a «formidable» city-state in 3400-3200 BC. It is reported in a press article about the announcement by the director of the excavation.

hechos/paleta-egipcia-de-khirbet-kerak/t.texto: Contacts with Egypt at Khirbet Kerak

hechos/paleta-egipcia-de-khirbet-kerak/r.texto: A stone palette with Egyptian motifs, including an ankh, found in 2009 at the tell, points to relations with the First Dynasty of Egypt around 3000 BC.

hechos/biblos-templo-de-baalat-gebal/tit.texto: Temple of Baalat Gebal at Byblos

hechos/biblos-templo-de-baalat-gebal/res.texto: Around 2800 BC the temple of Baalat Gebal, the city's goddess, was built at Byblos; it was the largest and most important sanctuary of Byblos and one of the first monumental structures in Syria and Palestine.

hechos/silabario-de-biblos/resumen.texto: Fourteen inscriptions in bronze and stone, found by Maurice Dunand in 1928-1932, are written in an undeciphered syllabic system, dated between the 18th and 15th centuries BC.

hechos/tradicion-de-los-patriarcas/resum.texto: The Hebrew Bible says that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lived in Canaan and Egypt. The account was composed centuries later, and there are no contemporary inscriptions naming the patriarchs; the date is a convention of the tradition.

hechos/salida-de-egipto-tradicion/titulo.texto: The exodus from Egypt according to biblical tradition

hechos/salida-de-egipto-tradicion/resume.texto: The Book of Exodus tells of the departure of the Israelites from Egypt, led by Moses. Archaeology has found no traces of a mass exodus, and scholarship debates whether there was an event behind the account, of what size and when; the date c. 1250 BC is one of the proposals.

hechos/conquista-de-canaan-segun-josue/t.texto: The conquest of Canaan according to the Book of Joshua

hechos/conquista-de-canaan-segun-josue/r.texto: The Book of Joshua tells of the conquest of Canaan by the Israelites in campaigns from Jericho. Most scholars see it as non-historical and think Israel emerged gradually within Canaanite society; the date is conventional.

hechos/caida-de-jerico-segun-josue/titul.texto: The fall of Jericho according to the Book of Joshua

hechos/caida-de-jerico-segun-josue/resum.texto: According to Joshua 6, the walls of Jericho fell after the Israelites marched around them. There is evidence of a city at the end of the Bronze Age, but there is consensus that the account arose from the political aims of much later kings of Judah.

hechos/jabin-rey-de-hazor-segun-josue/ti.texto: Jabin, king of Hazor, according to the Book of Joshua

hechos/jabin-rey-de-hazor-segun-josue/re.texto: The Book of Joshua tells that King Jabin of Hazor led a northern coalition defeated by the Israelites, who then burned Hazor. Norman Gottwald reads it as a reflection of the destruction of Hazor at the end of the 13th century BC by a group later identified with the tribe of Naphtali.

hechos/cultura-de-philia/resumen.texto: The Philia culture marks the beginning of the Early Bronze Age in Cyprus, between 2450 and 2200 BC, and takes its name from a place in Morphou.

hechos/silabario-chipro-minoico/resumen.texto: It was used in Cyprus and among its trading partners from c. 1550 to c. 1050 BC (between 1500 and 1150 BC according to others); it has not been deciphered. About 250 inscribed objects are known, among them the longest tablet, from Enkomi.

hechos/lingotes-de-cobre-de-chipre/titul.texto: Copper ingots in the shape of an oxhide

hechos/lingotes-de-cobre-de-chipre/resum.texto: They were produced in Cyprus, and the Amarna letters speak of the copper of Alashiya, whose capital has not been identified (Enkomi is the nearest site). Metal plates of 20 to 30 kg, of copper and sometimes tin, with four handles at the corners that made transport easier; they were produced and distributed in the Mediterranean of the Late Bronze Age.

hechos/fundicion-de-apliki/resumen.texto: At Apliki, from the late 14th century BC, there was a smelting site on rocky terraces; in four excavated houses a cylinder of ivory, a steatite seal and a gold earring were found.

hechos/palacio-de-alassa/resumen.texto: Between 1340 and 1100 BC the island's highest settlement was built on a plateau above the Kouris River, with a 1410 m² building around a central courtyard; it has been proposed as the capital of Alashiya.

hechos/auge-de-hala-sultan-tekke/titulo.texto: Hala Sultan Tekke, Late Bronze Age port city

hechos/auge-de-hala-sultan-tekke/resumen.texto: Radar surveys from 2010 to 2012 showed that this city of c. 1600-1100 BC was one of the largest of the Late Bronze Age, perhaps 50 hectares; the tombs found contain objects from 1500 and 1350 BC.

hechos/destruccion-de-kition/titulo.texto: Destruction of the Mycenaean settlement at Kition

hechos/destruccion-de-kition/resumen.texto: According to the literature, in the Late Bronze Age Mycenaean Greeks settled Kition and exploited the copper deposits (the Mycenaean presence in Cyprus is debated); the settlement was destroyed around 1200 BC and rebuilt shortly after on a larger scale, with a Cyclopean wall.

hechos/pyla-kokkinokremos-hecho/resumen.texto: Fortified plateau 10 km east of Larnaca, with seven densely occupied hectares, abandoned after a short occupation in the time of Enkomi and Kition (13th-12th centuries BC).

hechos/campanas-hititas-en-alashiya/resu.texto: According to a tablet from the time of Suppiluliuma II, Tudhaliya IV (c. 1245-1215 BC) took the king of Alashiya and made him tributary around 1225 BC; around 1195 BC a fleet of Suppiluliuma II (c. 1207-1178 BC) defeated another off the island, the first recorded naval battle. The capital of Alashiya has not been identified; Enkomi is the nearest documented site.

hechos/periodo-hafit/resumen.texto: In the UAE and Oman, at the beginning of the Bronze Age, the Hafit people built beehive-shaped tombs, with a small chamber for one or two burials, at places such as Jebel Hafit and Bat.

hechos/cobre-de-bat/titulo.texto: Copper and stone trade at Bat

hechos/cobre-de-bat/resumen.texto: Around 3000 BC at Bat, locally mined copper and stone, probably diorite, were traded with the Sumerians.

hechos/templo-de-barbar/resumen.texto: Three superimposed temples at Barbar: the second was built some 500 years after the first (c. 3000 BC) and the third between 2100 and 2000 BC; it was built with limestone blocks from the island of Jidda.

hechos/cultura-umm-an-nar/resumen.texto: Early Bronze Age culture of the UAE and Oman (c. 2600-2000 BC), a commercial intermediary between Sumer and the Indus valley; it is known from round stone tombs, such as those of Hili, and from settlements such as Tell Abraq.

hechos/magan-fuente-de-cobre/titulo.texto: Magan, source of copper and diorite for Mesopotamia

hechos/magan-fuente-de-cobre/resumen.texto: Sumerian texts of c. 2300 BC mention Magan, in present-day Oman and the UAE, as a supplier of copper and diorite; it was famous for its ships. Trade with the Indus passed through Magan.

hechos/torre-de-tell-abraq/resumen.texto: Around 2200 BC a circular tower of mudbrick and stone, about 40 m in diameter and 8 m high, was built at Tell Abraq; nearby there was an Umm an-Nar tomb with the remains of some 410 people.

hechos/cultura-wadi-suq/resumen.texto: It succeeded Umm an-Nar in the UAE and Oman, from 2000 to 1300 BC; the change was once explained by external catastrophes, but today it is seen more as a gradual social change.

hechos/apogeo-de-dilmun/resumen.texto: From c. 2050 BC Dilmun reached its peak and perhaps became a kingdom independent of Mesopotamia; Qal'at al-Bahrain was probably its capital, and it controlled the trade routes of the Persian Gulf.

hechos/declive-de-dilmun/resumen.texto: From c. 1720 BC many settlements went out of use, construction of royal burial mounds ceased, and the temple of Barbar fell into ruin; around 1650 BC there was a recovery, with new mounds and more building at Qal'at al-Bahrain.
