hechos/dilmun-bajo-mesopotamia/resumen.texto: From at least 1500 BC Dilmun was probably under the Sealand dynasty, which spoke Akkadian: a text from Qal'at al-Bahrain mentions its king Ea-gamil. It later passed to the Kassite dynasty of Babylon.

hechos/failaka-colonia-de-dilmun/resumen.texto: Failaka Island was settled after 2000 BC, after a fall in sea level, by merchants from Ur; a seal of c. 1650 BC preserves the name of a king of Dilmun.

hechos/zimri-lim-visita-ugarit/resumen.texto: Mari texts of c. 1765 BC mention Ugarit; Zimri-Lim, who reigned between c. 1775 and 1760 BC, made a state visit to the city, which was part of a trade route between Ugarit, Aleppo, Emar, Mari and Babylon.

hechos/ugarit-vasalla-de-yamhad/titulo.texto: Ugarit as a vassal of Yamhad

hechos/ugarit-vasalla-de-yamhad/resumen.texto: Around 1820 BC the great kingdom of Yamhad became a regional power under Sumu-Epuh, and Ugarit (stratum 7) ended up as its vassal, along with other kingdoms of the northern Levant.

hechos/templos-de-baal-y-dagan/titulo.texto: Temples of Baal and Dagan on the acropolis of Ugarit

hechos/templos-de-baal-y-dagan/resumen.texto: On the acropolis of Ugarit stood the main temples, of Baal and of his father Dagan, both with a portico and a sanctuary; what survives is from the Late Bronze Age, though they may have Middle Bronze Age origins. In the House of the High Priest, west of the temple of Dagan, tablets with mythological poems were found.

hechos/templo-de-hadad-de-alepo-hecho/ti.texto: Discovery of the temple of Hadad in the citadel of Aleppo

hechos/templo-de-hadad-de-alepo-hecho/re.texto: A temple of the storm god Hadad, recently found on the citadel hill, was in use from the 24th century BC and is mentioned in texts from Ebla and Mari; Aleppo, capital of Yamhad, was called «ciudad de Hadad» («city of Hadad»).

hechos/sweyhat-fortificaciones-y-tumbas/.texto: Fortifications and tombs of Tell es-Sweyhat

Tell es-Sweyhat is known for its intact walls from the middle and late third millennium and a temple from the end of the millennium on its summit; in 1993 a cemetery of shaft-and-chamber tombs from the middle of the third millennium was found in the mound beneath it.

hechos/hammam-et-turkman-muralla/titulo.texto: Early Bronze Age wall of Tell Hammam et-Turkman

hechos/hammam-et-turkman-muralla/resumen.texto: The city of EB III-IV in the Balikh valley was surrounded by an 8 m wide wall with upper chambers, dated by radiocarbon to around 2400 BC.

hechos/tell-touqan-ursaum/resumen.texto: The site, 15 km northwest of Ebla, has been identified with the city of Ursa'um, an important regional center in the 24th century BC; in the Early Bronze IVB it was part of the kingdom of Ebla.

hechos/tumba-comunal-de-tell-tweini/resu.texto: Among the most notable finds at this site, which may have been Gibala, a coastal city in the southern part of the kingdom of Ugarit, is a communal tomb from c. 1700 BC.

hechos/destruccion-de-tell-sukas/resumen.texto: A layer of ash at Tell Sukas, probably Suksi, was interpreted as a violent destruction around 1170 BC, as at other coastal sites, among them Tell Tweini and Ugarit; unlike them, the site was not abandoned.

hechos/ceramica-chipriota-en-tell-kazel/.texto: At Tell Kazel, a city of Amurru, much Cypriot bichrome pottery from the 14th to 12th centuries BC was found, unlike other sites on the Homs Gap; after the Late Bronze Age destruction it was replaced by local Mycenaean pottery and hand-burnished pottery.

hechos/archivo-cuneiforme-de-hazor/resum.texto: Hazor yielded more cuneiform tablets than any other site in the southern Levant: those from the Middle Bronze Age are in standard Old Babylonian Akkadian, and those from the Late Bronze Age are in a local dialect similar to that of the Amarna letters.

hechos/edificio-negro-de-hazor/resumen.texto: On the acropolis of Hazor, monumental Late Bronze Age structures combine the functions of palace and temple, with a «Ceremonial Palace» and a large throne room, the «Black Building», in the Syrian architectural tradition. The date within the Late Bronze Age is approximate.

hechos/biridiya-y-meguido/titulo.texto: Biridiya of Megiddo writes to the pharaoh

hechos/biridiya-y-meguido/resumen.texto: Biridiya, ruler of Megiddo and vassal of Egypt, wrote five letters to the pharaoh, which show him caught up in the intrigues of Labayu.

hechos/suwardata-contra-los-habiru/titul.texto: Šuwardata of Gath reports his victory over the habiru

hechos/suwardata-contra-los-habiru/resum.texto: In letter EA 366, the king of Gath informs the pharaoh that he put down a habiru rebellion.

hechos/laquis-bronce-medio/titulo.texto: Lachish, a large city of the Middle Bronze IIB-C

hechos/laquis-bronce-medio/resumen.texto: Between 1630 and 1550 BC Lachish became a large city of the southern Levant, with a glacis structure around its perimeter, a wall of large stones and a mudbrick fortress.

hechos/destruccion-de-laquis-bronce-tard.texto: Destruction of Lachish at the end of the Late Bronze Age

There is archaeological evidence of one or two violent destructions at Lachish at the end of the 13th or beginning of the 12th century BC; there is no conclusive historical evidence about who was responsible, and internal Canaanite conflicts were proposed among other explanations.

hechos/jerico-bronce-medio/titulo.texto: Jericho at its greatest extent in the Middle Bronze Age

hechos/jerico-bronce-medio/resumen.texto: Jericho, a small prominent city of Canaan, reached its greatest extent in the Bronze Age in 1700-1550 BC, with walls and towers and an extensive cemetery of shaft tombs; it has been linked to the rise of the maryannu.

hechos/jerico-bronce-tardio/titulo.texto: Destruction of Jericho at the end of the Bronze Age

hechos/jerico-bronce-tardio/resumen.texto: Jericho was destroyed in the Late Bronze Age and ceased to be an urban center. The date of the destruction and its relation to the biblical account in Joshua are debated: there is consensus that the biblical account is not strict history.

hechos/tell-el-ajjul-sucesora-de-tell-es.texto: Tell el-Ajjul, successor of Tell es-Sakan

Tell el-Ajjul was founded about 500 meters south of Tell es-Sakan, abandoned in the 23rd century BC; Pierre de Miroschedji and Moain Sadeq propose it as its successor, and Aharon Kempinski proposes it as Sharuhen, the last Hyksos fortress around 1550 BC.

hechos/excavacion-de-tell-el-hesi/titulo.texto: First stratigraphic excavation at Tell el-Hesi

hechos/excavacion-de-tell-el-hesi/resume.texto: The Palestine Exploration Fund excavated Tell el-Hesi in five seasons in 1890-1892, the first with Flinders Petrie and the following ones with Frederick Bliss, who applied Petrie's pottery sequence in a layer-by-layer excavation.

hechos/derrota-de-mari-ante-ebla-siglo-x.texto: Defeat of Mari by Ebla in the 25th century BC

The archives of Ebla record a defeat of Mari in the 25th century BC. According to Alfonso Archi's estimates of the reigns, the Eblaite king who caused it may have been Kun-Damu, though the texts do not say so.

hechos/colonia-de-mari-en-tunip/titulo.texto: Mari colony in Tunip under Ebla's hegemony

hechos/colonia-de-mari-en-tunip/resumen.texto: In the archive of Palace G at Ebla, Tunip appears under that city's hegemony, with a colony of at least 530 men from Mari led by Puzur-Aštar: 30 merchants and their workers, who probably obtained timber from the nearby mountains.

hechos/abdi-ashirta-contra-rib-hadda/tit.texto: Abdi-Ashirta of Amurru against Rib-Hadda of Byblos

hechos/abdi-ashirta-contra-rib-hadda/res.texto: In the Amarna letters Rib-Hadda accuses Abdi-Ashirta of hiring habiru and shardana mercenaries, of drawing his followers into rebellion (EA 81), and of sending an assassin against him, and he asks Egypt for help. Recent studies hold that Amurru was then a decentralized land of several independent entities, over which Abdi-Ashirta had influence without governing them directly.

hechos/aziru-toma-sumur/resumen.texto: Aziru, son and successor of Abdi-Ashirta, sought to extend Amurru toward the Mediterranean coast and took the city of Sumur. This alarmed his neighbors, especially Rib-Hadda of Byblos, who asked for Egyptian troops.

hechos/aziru-retenido-en-egipto/titulo.texto: Aziru, summoned to Egypt, is detained

hechos/aziru-retenido-en-egipto/resumen.texto: The pharaoh Akhenaten, in letter EA 162, required Aziru to travel to Egypt to explain his actions. Aziru was detained for at least a year and returned to Amurru when the Hittites took Amqu (the Biqa), which threatened his kingdom.

hechos/vasallaje-de-aziru-con-suppiluliu.texto: Aziru becomes a vassal of Suppiluliuma I

Aziru definitively changed his loyalty to Suppiluliuma I after returning from Egypt, around 1340-1335 BC, and remained faithful to the Hittites until his death; the treaty is known as CTH 49. Amurru remained in Hittite hands until the reigns of Seti I and Ramesses II.

hechos/carta-de-tunip-e-irqata-al-faraon.texto: Tunip and Irqata write to the pharaoh

Among the Amarna letters, only those of Tunip (EA 59) and Irqata (EA 100) were sent by a city rather than by its ruler. Both speak of the city's guard, of the war with the habiru and of its loyalty, and ask Egypt for protection.

hechos/tablillas-de-taanach-hecho/resume.texto: Thirteen cuneiform tablets of the 15th century BC, twelve of them in Akkadian, document the correspondence of Reshawur, king of Taanach at the end of the 15th century BC, with neighboring kings and with an official assumed to be an Egyptian representative in Gaza; a third of the names are Hurrian or northern. Taanach also appears in Papyrus Petersburg 1116A among the cities that sent Canaanite envoys to the pharaoh Amenhotep II.

hechos/archivo-de-urtenu-hecho/titulo.texto: Archive of the house of Urtenu in Ugarit

hechos/archivo-de-urtenu-hecho/resumen.texto: The house of Urtenu kept tablets from the last reigns of Ugarit: legal texts, Hittite letters about tribute, and a clay tag with the seal of Ammurapi. Among the letters is one from the Hittite queen mother Puduheba, who reproaches Niqmaddu III for not visiting the court or paying the tribute.

hechos/notacion-musical-hurrita-de-ugari.texto: Around 1400 BC some 36 Hurrian songs were written at Ugarit, on cuneiform tablets from the royal palace, of which only one, the Hymn to Nikkal (h.6), survives almost complete. It is the oldest notated music known to survive almost whole; its modern reconstruction has changed over the years.

hechos/divorcio-de-ammittamru-ii/titulo.texto: Ammittamru II repudiates his wife from Amurru

hechos/divorcio-de-ammittamru-ii/resumen.texto: Ammittamru II of Ugarit repudiated his wife Piddu, daughter of Benteshina of Amurru, for a serious offense, and demanded her extradition; his brother Shaushgamuwa of Amurru refused, fearing she would be executed. The great Hittite king Tudhaliya IV (from c. 1245 BC) intervened to halt the conflict between two vassals, and the Karkemish viceroy Ini-Teššup ruled that she was to be extradited and that Šaušgamuwa should receive 1400 shekels of gold.

hechos/destierro-de-principes-de-ugarit-.texto: Ahatmilku exiles two sons to Alashiya
After the death of Niqmepa, his widow Ahatmilku backed the succession of her son Ammittamru II. When two of her sons contested it, she exiled them to Alashiya, on Cyprus, with sufficient provisions.

hechos/terremoto-de-enkomi/resumen.texto: Excavators date to around 1400 BC the destruction by earthquake of Enkomi's Level I, which had begun slowly around 1550 BC and was flourishing around 1500 BC, in the Late Cypriot I-II period.

hechos/enkomi-centro-del-cobre/titulo.texto: Enkomi, center of copper smelting and trade

hechos/enkomi-centro-del-cobre/resumen.texto: From the 16th to the 12th century BC Enkomi was an important center of copper trade, with the metal smelted on the site itself, and strong cultural ties with Ugarit, on the Syrian coast opposite. Some propose that it was the Alashiya of the Amarna letters.

hechos/destruccion-masiva-de-enkomi/titu.texto: Massive destruction of Enkomi around 1220 BC

hechos/destruccion-masiva-de-enkomi/resu.texto: According to the excavators, Enkomi's Level II, with its great expansion in the 14th and 13th centuries BC, ends in a massive destruction around 1220 BC; it is followed by Level III, with Mycenaean settlers.

hechos/destruccion-de-enkomi-iii/titulo.texto: Last destructive attack on Enkomi around 1125 BC

hechos/destruccion-de-enkomi-iii/resumen.texto: Enkomi's Level III, with Mycenaean settlers, includes a destructive attack, possibly related to the Sea Peoples, and ends in a destruction around 1125 BC; the final phase, IIIC, had a declining population.

hechos/dor-y-los-tjekker/titulo.texto: Dor and the Tjekker after the collapse

hechos/dor-y-los-tjekker/resumen.texto: After the collapse of the Late Bronze Age, Dor was settled by a group called the Tjekker. In the account of Wenamun, the protagonist visits Dor and is received by a Tjekker prince named Beder; this level, Dor XII, is dated to around 1150-1050 BC and ends in a violent fire that Ephraim Stern links to the Phoenician conquest of the Tjekker.

hechos/et-tell-ciudad-del-bronce-antiguo.texto: Fortified city of Et-Tell (Ai) in the Early Bronze Age

Et-Tell had a large fortified city between c. 3100 and 2400 BC, with cycles of destruction and rebuilding, and was then abandoned; excavations found no Middle or Late Bronze Age occupation. The site is commonly identified with Ai, which the Book of Joshua says was conquered by the Israelites; because of this mismatch, many scholars read the account as etiological, and Albright's positivist reading, which saw it as proof of the conquest, was later challenged.

hechos/destruccion-hicsa-de-tel-beit-she.texto: Hyksos-period destruction of Tel Beit Shemesh
In the 17th century BC Tel Beit Shemesh had a massive fortification with a south gate, and in the Middle Bronze IIC (c. 1590-1550 BC), in the Hyksos period, a destruction layer.

hechos/ashdod-ciudad-cananea/resumen.texto: The first documented urban settlement at Tel Ashdod dates to the 17th century BC, when it was a fortified Canaanite city; it was destroyed at the end of the Late Bronze Age.

hechos/puerto-de-ras-al-jinz/titulo.texto: Ras al-Jinz port and trade with the Indus

hechos/puerto-de-ras-al-jinz/resumen.texto: The Bronze Age port of Ras al-Jinz, on the east coast of Oman, had a mudbrick workshop where shells, turtle shell and cosmetics were processed. About 20% of its pottery came from the Indus valley, with sherds bearing signs of the Indus script, which shows overseas trade; bitumen with reed impressions provides information about the ships called Magan ships.

hechos/inscripcion-de-ramses-iii-en-taym.texto: Inscription of Ramesses III near Tayma

In 2010 a hieroglyphic inscription of Ramesses III (r. 1184-1153 BC) was found about 60 km northwest of Tayma, the first of its kind in Saudi Arabia. It is linked to Ramesside Egyptian hegemony over the area at the beginning of the Iron Age.

hechos/fortificacion-de-tel-zeror/titulo.texto: Wall and ditch of Tel Zeror

hechos/fortificacion-de-tel-zeror/resume.texto: In the Middle Bronze IIA the city of Tel Zeror was surrounded by an earthen, mudbrick and stone wall 4.5 m wide, with a watchtower, and by a ditch 10 m wide. The site seems to have been abandoned from the 18th century BC and was not resettled until the early 15th century BC.

hechos/fortaleza-de-tel-mevorakh/titulo.texto: Middle Bronze fortress of Tel Mevorakh

hechos/fortaleza-de-tel-mevorakh/resumen.texto: In the Middle Bronze IIB (stratum XIII) Tel Mevorakh was surrounded by a high earthen rampart, a typical feature of Canaanite fortification of the period, and a fortress or garrison was built at the center of the mound, in use until the end of the Middle Bronze Age.

hechos/plataforma-de-tel-michal/resumen.texto: The first settlers of Tel Michal, at the end of the Middle Bronze IIB, built a 4 m high platform of alternating layers of red clay and sand, held up on the north by a brick wall and a sloping sand glacis.

hechos/destruccion-de-tell-keisan/titulo.texto: Destruction of Tell Keisan around the 12th century BC

hechos/destruccion-de-tell-keisan/resume.texto: In the Late Bronze Age Tell Keisan was a much smaller settlement than in the Early and Middle Bronze Ages, and a destruction level is identified from the beginning of the 12th century BC.

hechos/asentamiento-hicso-de-tell-el-far.texto: From the Middle Bronze IIB-IIC/III, around 1600 BC, the site had a town with fortifications, a gate and a ditch, generally identified as Hyksos. Albright proposed it as Sharuhen; by around 1550 BC many cities of southern Canaan had passed under direct Egyptian control or become vassals.

hechos/muwatalli-ii-depone-a-bentesina/t.texto: Muwatalli II deposes Benteshina and reorganizes Amurru

hechos/muwatalli-ii-depone-a-bentesina/r.texto: In year 4 of Ramesses II, when the Egyptians invaded Amurru, Benteshina was on the throne and did not resist: he defected to the Egyptians. After the battle of Qadesh (year 5), Muwatalli II recovered Qadesh and Amurru, deposed Benteshina and put Šapili in his place, who remained until Hattusili III came to the throne.

hechos/tratado-de-hattusili-iii-con-bent.texto: Treaty of Hattusili III with Benteshina of Amurru

When Hattusili III came to the throne, Šapili was removed and Benteshina became king of Amurru again, as vassal of the Hittite great king. The treaty, catalogued as CTH 92, sets out that relationship.

hechos/estatua-de-ibbit-lim-hallada/titu.texto: Discovery of the statue of Ibbit-Lim

hechos/estatua-de-ibbit-lim-hallada/resu.texto: In 1968 Italian archaeologists from the University of Rome La Sapienza found at Tell Mardikh a votive statue dedicated to Ishtar in the name of Ibbit-Lim, king of Ebla, and this identified the site with ancient Ebla.

hechos/inscripcion-protocananea-de-laqui.texto: An ivory comb of c. 1700 BC, found at Tel Lachish in 2016, bears a Proto-Canaanite inscription whose letters resemble the Proto-Sinaitic ones; it was deciphered in 2022. The Lachish jar of the late 13th century BC carries another, an offering to Asherah. About 20 to 25 Proto-Canaanite inscriptions are known.

lugares/ebla/resumen.texto: City of northwestern Syria, about 55 km southwest of Aleppo, a center of the Levant in the third millennium BC and in the first half of the second. Palace G of the first kingdom was destroyed around 2300 BC (with its tablet archive), and the city was razed for the last time around 1600 BC; afterward it was a small village.

lugares/tell-banat/resumen.texto: Bronze Age site on the middle Euphrates, in northern Syria, with two mounds; its funerary finds are considered unique in Upper Mesopotamia.

lugares/tell-hadidi/resumen.texto: Site on the Syrian Euphrates, on the west bank of the river opposite Tell es-Sweyhat, occupied from the Early Bronze Age to the Late Bronze Age; its main god was Dagan, and the two probably controlled a river crossing together. The coordinate is approximate.

lugares/tell-es-sweyhat/resumen.texto: Large site on the Syrian Euphrates, about 45 hectares, occupied from 3100 to 1900 BC. It is known for its third-millennium walls, a temple from the end of that millennium, and a cemetery of shaft-and-chamber tombs.

lugares/emar/resumen.texto: City on the Syrian Euphrates, at a bend of the river, which under Hittite rule was the capital of the province of Astata. Its cuneiform tablets from the 14th to 12th centuries BC place it alongside Ugarit, Mari and Ebla among the great finds of Syria; the city fell in 1187 BC.

lugares/tell-fray/resumen.texto: Site on the Syrian Euphrates with occupation from the 14th century BC, temples and officials' houses, within the sphere of Astata and Emar. A fire in the 13th century BC destroyed it, perhaps at the hands of Shalmaneser I or Tukulti-Ninurta I.

lugares/mumbaqat/resumen.texto: Site on the Syrian Euphrates proposed as the Late Bronze Age city of Ekalte, with four known temples; its city god was Baʿlaka.

lugares/umm-el-marra/resumen.texto: City of the Jabbul Plain, northwest of Ebla, which was an important center of the Early Bronze III with 3000 to 5000 inhabitants and, after the Middle Bronze renewal, a regional capital subject to Yamhad. It was destroyed in the 14th century BC, after Hittite rule, and was completely abandoned around 1200-1190 BC.

lugares/tell-afis/resumen.texto: Site about 11 km north of Ebla, on the road to Aleppo, occupied since the Chalcolithic; in the Middle Bronze IIA it was under the control of Yamhad. In the Iron Age it was the city of Hazrek.

lugares/alalakh/resumen.texto: City of the Amuq Valley, beside the Orontes, in present-day Hatay province, Turkey, which flourished in the Middle and Late Bronze Ages with palaces, temples, walls and houses. It depended on Yamhad, Mitanni and the Hittites, and was the seat of the kingdom of Mukish.

lugares/qatna/resumen.texto: City 18 km northeast of Homs, a center of the second millennium BC and capital of a regional kingdom from c. 2000 BC. It had one of the largest royal palaces in Syria, of 16,000 m², and an intact royal tomb. After the destruction of the 14th century BC the city shrank and was abandoned by the 13th century BC; it was resettled in the 10th century BC.

lugares/ugarit/resumen.texto: Coastal city of northern Syria, about 10 km north of Latakia, occupied from the end of the eighth millennium BC. Its apogee was between 1500 and 1200 BC; it was a port trading with Egypt, Cyprus and the Aegean, it produced the cuneiform alphabet, and it was destroyed around 1185 BC.

lugares/palacio-real-de-ugarit/resumen.texto: Residence of the kings of Ugarit, excavated by Claude Schaeffer from the 1930s and considered one of the main finds of the site; one of its tablet archives was found there.

lugares/minet-el-beida/resumen.texto: Bay about 10 km north of Latakia that was the main port of Ugarit; in antiquity it was called Maʾḫadu.

lugares/ras-ibn-hani/resumen.texto: Headland 8 km north of Latakia, occupied almost without interruption from the Late Bronze Age to the Byzantine period; it was the second port of Ugarit, called Raʾšu in the texts. Its occupation is dated from the mid-13th century BC; an alternative description puts it in the 14th century, and the site survived the fall of Ugarit.

lugares/tell-tweini/resumen.texto: Site of about 12 hectares south of Latakia, identified with Gibala, a port city on the southern border of the kingdom of Ugarit. A communal tomb from c. 1700 BC is one of its most notable finds.

lugares/tell-kazel/resumen.texto: Tell in the Akkar Plain, about 18 km south of Tartus, identified with Sumur, capital of Amurru. Its Cypriot pottery from the 14th to 12th centuries BC contrasts with other sites on the Homs Gap; the city was destroyed at the end of the Late Bronze Age.

lugares/qadesh/resumen.texto: City of the Levant on the upper Orontes, important in the Late Bronze Age and mentioned in the Amarna letters; it was the scene of the battle of Qadesh between Egypt and the Hittites in the 13th century BC.

lugares/gezer/resumen.texto: Fortified Canaanite city on the foothills of the Judean hills, halfway between Jerusalem and the coast, which was an important state in the first half of the second millennium BC. It appears in Egyptian inscriptions and in the Amarna letters, with the rulers Milkilu, Yapahu and Adda-danu.

lugares/siquem/resumen.texto: City of the central highlands of Canaan, which remained occupied in the Iron Age and later. Its first large construction dates to the Middle Bronze IIA, around 1900 BC, and the stela of Sesostris III's Sebek-khu mentions it as attacked by Egypt; in the Amarna letters it is the seat of Labayu.

lugares/beit-shean/resumen.texto: City in the Beit Shean valley, 120 m below sea level, occupied from the Early Bronze IB (c. 3300-3050 BC), with a break in EB II; it resumes in EB IIIA, and there is a possible gap in EB IIIB-IV because of drought.

lugares/tel-kabri/resumen.texto: Tell of western Galilee with one of the largest Canaanite palaces of the Middle Bronze Age (2100-1550 BC), the largest excavated up to 2014. Its original Canaanite name is unknown.

lugares/tel-arad/resumen.texto: City of the eastern Negev, occupied from the late Chalcolithic; in the Early Bronze II it was a large fortified city with Egyptian imports. Its last Bronze Age stratum, a scattered village, was abandoned around 2650 BC; afterward there was a 1500-year gap until the 10th-century BC fortress of Judah.

lugares/bab-edh-dhra/resumen.texto: Early Bronze Age city southeast of the Dead Sea, on the south bank of Wadi Kerak. Its cemetery, with about 20,000 shaft tombs and ossuaries, is one of the largest in the region; the city was abandoned around 2350 BC.

lugares/numeira/resumen.texto: Early Bronze Age site on the shore of the Dead Sea, in Jordan, violently destroyed at the end of EB III and never resettled.

lugares/tel-dan/resumen.texto: Tell in northern Israel, occupied since the late Neolithic. A mudbrick gate of c. 1750 BC with three true arches is among the oldest complete monumental arches; Egyptian Middle Kingdom execration texts curse Laish.

lugares/tel-afek/resumen.texto: Archaeological site in the coastal interior of Israel, in the Ein Afek reserve east of Kiryat Bialik, also called Tel Kurdani.

lugares/taanach/resumen.texto: Canaanite city of the Jezreel Valley, a fortified city in the Early Bronze IIIA (c. 2750-2500 BC). It appears on a papyrus of Amenhotep II and in the Amarna letters, where it is ruled by a minor king.

lugares/pella/resumen.texto: City on the eastern slope of the Jordan Valley, occupied since the Neolithic; around 3400 BC it was a walled city. In the Amarna letters it is the seat of the ruler Mutbaal.

lugares/tell-el-ajjul/resumen.texto: Tell at the mouth of Wadi Ghazzah, south of the city of Gaza, with a fortified city occupied in the Bronze Age (c. 2000-1800 BC onward). It is the successor of Tell es-Sakan, abandoned in the 23rd century BC, and has been proposed as Sharuhen.

lugares/tell-el-hesi/resumen.texto: Tell of the southern Shephelah with its main occupation in the Early Bronze Age; around 2750-2500 BC it was a fortified city of 10 hectares. There Flinders Petrie and then Frederick Bliss developed stratigraphic excavation in 1890-1892.

lugares/tell-beit-mirsim/resumen.texto: Shephelah site with ten or eleven strata from the late third millennium to c. 589 BC; its pottery by stratum is a reference for the archaeology of Israel.

lugares/tell-jemmeh/resumen.texto: Tell in the Besor stream bed, occupied from the Chalcolithic and again from the Middle Bronze II (c. 1800 BC) for about 1600 years; it is identified with Yursa.

lugares/tell-es-safi/resumen.texto: Large Shephelah tell on the south bank of the Wadi Ajjur, with 24 hectares of Early Bronze Age occupation; it is identified with Gath of the Philistines, and by most scholars with the city whose king Šuwardata writes in the Amarna letters.

lugares/tel-yarmuth/resumen.texto: Shephelah tell, heavily occupied in the Early Bronze II and III and abandoned around 2400 BC; only the acropolis saw minor later occupations, among them Mycenaean and Cypriot pottery of the 13th century BC.

lugares/khirbet-kerak/resumen.texto: Tell of more than 50 hectares on the south shore of the Sea of Galilee, with Early Bronze Age occupation (c. 3300/3500-2200 BC). A stone palette with Egyptian motifs suggests ties with the First Dynasty around 3000 BC.

lugares/tell-abu-al-kharaz/resumen.texto: Tell in the Jordan Valley in Jordan, with fortified cities of the Early, Middle and Late Bronze Ages; its largest phase was in the Early Bronze Age, around 3000 BC.

lugares/enkomi/resumen.texto: Second-millennium BC site on the east coast of Cyprus, the main center of the Late Bronze Age, where Cypro-Minoan inscriptions were found, among them the longest known clay tablet; some propose it as the capital of Alashiya.

lugares/kition/resumen.texto: City-kingdom on the south coast of Cyprus, at present-day Larnaca. According to the literature, in the Late Bronze Age Mycenaean Greeks settled it and exploited local copper (this is debated); that settlement was destroyed around 1200 BC and rebuilt on a larger scale shortly after.

lugares/hala-sultan-tekke/resumen.texto: Large Late Bronze Age port city beside the salt lake of Larnaca (c. 1600-1100 BC), which according to radar surveys reached about 50 hectares. Centuries later the mosque that gives the site its name was built beside it.

lugares/pyla-kokkinokremos/resumen.texto: Fortified Late Bronze Age settlement on a rocky plateau 10 km east of Larnaca, briefly occupied and then abandoned; densely built on about seven hectares.

lugares/alassa/resumen.texto: Settlement in southwestern Cyprus, on the Kouris River, built between c. 1340 and 1100 BC, with monumental buildings suggesting an important local center; it has been proposed as the capital of Alashiya.

lugares/apliki/resumen.texto: Late Bronze Age copper mining region in northern Cyprus, with a smelting site on rocky terraces and rich houses, from the late 14th century BC.

lugares/dilmun-barbar/resumen.texto: Complex of three superimposed temples at Barbar, Bahrain, of the Dilmun culture; the oldest date to c. 3000 BC and the third was added between 2100 and 2000 BC. It was discovered by the Dane P. V. Glob in 1954; the temple fell into ruin after 1720 BC.

lugares/tumulos-de-dilmun/resumen.texto: Necropolis on the main island of Bahrain, from the Dilmun and Umm an-Nar cultures, one of the largest cemeteries of the ancient world, with thousands of mounds concentrated in the north of the island.

lugares/bat-al-khutm-al-ayn/resumen.texto: Group of beehive tombs and a necropolis of the Hafit period of the third millennium BC, in Oman, beside a palm grove. Around 3000 BC locally mined copper and stone, perhaps diorite, were traded there with the Sumerians.

lugares/jebel-hafit/resumen.texto: Mountain on the border of the UAE and Oman, next to Al Ain, where the beehive tombs that give the Hafit period its name (c. 3200-2600 BC) were found.

lugares/tell-abraq/resumen.texto: Settlement on the border of Sharjah and Umm al-Quwain, occupied from c. 2200 BC by the Umm an-Nar, Wadi Suq and Iron Age cultures, with a circular tower 40 m in diameter from c. 2200 BC and a tomb with the remains of some 410 people.

lugares/shimal/resumen.texto: Settlement in Ras al-Khaimah with an important archaeological site of the Umm an-Nar culture (2600-2000 BC).

lugares/tell-hammam-et-turkman/resumen.texto: Tell 500 m in diameter and 45 m high in the Balikh valley, north of Raqqa, occupied from the Northern Ubaid period (c. 4400-3600 BC). The city of EB III-IV was surrounded by a wide wall dated to around 2400 BC.

lugares/tell-touqan/resumen.texto: Tell about 15 km northwest of Ebla, identified with the city of Ursa'um, a regional center of the 24th century BC; in the Early Bronze IVB it was part of the kingdom of Ebla.

lugares/tell-sukas/resumen.texto: Coastal tell about 6 km south of Jableh, from the Late Bronze Age, possibly the ancient Suksi, one of the southern ports of the kingdom of Ugarit; a layer of ash from c. 1170 BC is interpreted as a fire destruction.

lugares/tell-qarqur/resumen.texto: Large tell of the Ghab valley, in the Orontes valley, with 10,000 years of nearly continuous occupation; its greatest extent is from the Early Bronze Age (3000-2000 BC).

lugares/tell-el-hammam/resumen.texto: A large site of 36 hectares in the lower Jordan Valley, in Jordan, occupied since the Late Chalcolithic; it had walls in the Early Bronze Age and its greatest extent in the Middle Bronze Age. Its identification with the biblical Sodom is rejected by mainstream archaeology.

lugares/tell-arqa/resumen.texto: A tell near the Lebanese village of Arqa, about 22 km northeast of Tripoli, occupied since the Neolithic. In the Early Bronze IV it was one of the three great sites of the Akkar Plain, along with Tell Kazel and Tell Jamous; Irqata appears in the Amarna letters, among them a letter from the city itself to the pharaoh (EA 100).

lugares/sarepta/resumen.texto: Phoenician city on the Lebanese coast between Sidon and Tyre, the only city of the Phoenician heartland excavated thoroughly (James B. Pritchard, 1969-1974). It is first mentioned in the journey of an Egyptian of the 14th century BC. Occupied from c. 1600 BC.

lugares/tell-el-burak/resumen.texto: A tell near the south coast of Lebanon, a few kilometers from Sidon, with Middle Bronze, Iron Age and Ottoman occupations. Its Middle Bronze fortress is the first fortified palace of that period found in Lebanon, with mural paintings showing ties with Egypt from as early as c. 1900 BC (one of the proposed dates), and it fills a gap in the history of Sidon.

lugares/tel-beit-shemesh/resumen.texto: A small tell northwest of the present-day city of Beit Shemesh, identified since 1830 with the biblical Beth-Shemesh. In the Middle Bronze IIB it had a massive fortification with a south gate (17th century BC) and a destruction layer around 1590-1550 BC, in the Hyksos period.

lugares/tell-abu-hawam/resumen.texto: A small port town in the Bay of Haifa, founded in the Late Bronze Age around 1600 BC and excavated by a British expedition in 1929-1933. The Crusaders called it Old Haifa; its population moved at the end of the 11th century AD.

lugares/ashdod/resumen.texto: A Canaanite city on the southern coast, about 6 km southeast of present-day Ashdod. Its first documented urban settlement dates to the 17th century BC, as a fortified city, and it was destroyed at the end of the Late Bronze Age.

lugares/shiloh/resumen.texto: A walled Canaanite city with a sanctuary in the Middle and Late Bronze Age, in the hill country about 31 km north of Jerusalem. The Bible presents it as an Israelite cult center before the Temple; archaeology dates its destruction in Iron I, by radiocarbon, to the second half of the 11th century BC.

lugares/et-tell/resumen.texto: A site in the West Bank commonly identified with the biblical Ai. It had a fortified Early Bronze city between c. 3100 and 2400 BC, destroyed several times and abandoned at the end of Early Bronze III; excavations found no Middle or Late Bronze occupation, and the site remained uninhabited until a small Iron I village.

lugares/tel-rumeida/resumen.texto: A tell inside the city of Hebron, with remains from the Chalcolithic (c. 3500 BC) that are considered the Canaanite, Israelite and Edomite settlements of Hebron. It expanded in the Early Bronze III with a fortified area of more than 30 dunams, and in the Middle Bronze I-II (c. 2000-1600 BC) it was surrounded by cyclopean walls.

lugares/tel-dor/resumen.texto: A tell on the coast of Israel, about 30 km south of Haifa, identified with D-jr in Egyptian sources and with the biblical Dor; the city was founded in the Middle Bronze Age, around 2000 BC, and its documented history begins in the Late Bronze Age. After the collapse it was inhabited by the Tjekker, and stratum Dor XII (c. 1150-1050 BC) corresponds to the visit in the account of Wenamun; the city was destroyed by fire in the mid-11th century BC.

lugares/jawa/resumen.texto: A site in the basalt desert of eastern Jordan with the oldest proto-urban development in the country, from the late 4th millennium BC. It has the oldest known gravity dam, with an initial radiocarbon date of 3500-3400 BC, and a fortified building from around 2000-1500 BC.

lugares/tell-deir-alla/resumen.texto: A tell in the Jordan Valley, in Jordan, which from the Late Bronze Age (16th century BC) was a sanctuary and a metallurgical center surrounded by smelting furnaces. In 1964 clay tablets with early Canaanite writing were found in the destruction layer of its deposits, dated to around 1200 BC by a cartouche of Queen Tausert; the identification with Sukkot is not confirmed by any inscription.

lugares/tell-el-farah-norte/resumen.texto: A tell in the West Bank identified with the biblical Tirzah. In the Early Bronze Age it had walls, houses and a temple; its finds include the oldest two-chambered pottery kiln of its type, and there was continuity of occupation in the transition from Early Bronze I to II, around 3000 BC.

lugares/tel-haror/resumen.texto: A tell in the western Negev, on the Wadi Gerar; in the Middle Bronze IIB it was one of the largest urban centers of the area. It is identified with Gerar, and Anson Rainey and Donald Redford propose it as the Egyptian fortress of Sharuhen, taken by Ahmose I.

lugares/tall-bazi/resumen.texto: A site on the Syrian Euphrates, twin of the nearby Tell Banat, both occupied in the third and second millennia BC. The citadel and Tell Banat were destroyed around 2300 BC; in the Late Bronze Age it had a western quarter of about a hundred houses, and in the temple two tablets recording land donations from the Mitanni period were found.

lugares/tel-dothan/resumen.texto: A tell near Jenin, in the West Bank, a heavily fortified Canaanite city in the Early Bronze I-III (c. 3700-2300 BC). It was abandoned during the Early Bronze IV (c. 2350-2000 BC) until the Middle Bronze IIB.

lugares/tel-gerisa/resumen.texto: A tell of about 40 dunams on the south bank of the Yarkon, within present-day Tel Aviv, with main phases from the Middle and Late Bronze Ages and a minor later occupation. Its ancient name is unknown.

lugares/tunip/resumen.texto: A city of northern Syria, probably Tell Acharneh, which in the archive of Palace G at Ebla (c. 2400-2300 BC) was under Ebla's hegemony, with a colony of at least 530 men from Mari dedicated to the timber trade. It appears in five Amarna letters, among them one from its citizens to the pharaoh (EA 59) about the wars with the habiru.

lugares/maa-palaeokastro/resumen.texto: A fortified Late Bronze Age settlement on a peninsula in southwestern Cyprus, near Pegeia, occupied by Greeks from the late 13th to the mid-12th century BC. The finds indicate metalworking and trade; it was abandoned in the context of the Final Bronze Age collapse.

lugares/erimi/resumen.texto: Village in the Limassol district, near Kourion, with several archaeological sites: Erimi-Pamboula, of the Chalcolithic; Erimi-Kafkalla and Erimi-Laonin tou Porakou, of the Early and Middle Bronze Age; and Erimi-Pitharka, of the Late Bronze Age. Erimi-Pamboula is Chalcolithic, which in Cyprus begins around 3500 BC.

lugares/kourion/resumen.texto: A city-state in southwestern Cyprus, on the Kouris valley, which in the Late Bronze Age (1600-1050 BC) formed a complex urban center in the Troodos copper trade corridor, controlled from Alassa and Episkopi-Bamboula. In the 12th century BC, after the fall of the Mycenaean palaces, Greek settlers arrived from Argos.

lugares/idalion/resumen.texto: A Cypriot city-kingdom at present-day Dali, founded on copper trade in the third millennium BC. In the 13th century BC its people began producing on the south bank of the Yialias River, where the city grew into a large urban and copper-trading center.

lugares/palaepafos/resumen.texto: A Bronze Age settlement that gave its name to the kingdom of Paphos, in southwestern Cyprus; its founding as a town is dated to around 1700 BC near present-day Kouklia. It was an administrative, commercial and cult center, with the sanctuary of Aphrodite of Paphos, and it was called Palaepaphos when Nea Paphos was founded in the 4th century BC.

lugares/tamasos/resumen.texto: City-state in the interior of Cyprus, whose center is thought to lie beneath the village of Politiko. It prospered from its copper mines, which replaced small farming villages, and it had no port. Occupied since the Bronze Age, c. 2000 BC; mentioned as Tamesi around 673 BC.

lugares/lapithos/resumen.texto: A city on the north coast of Cyprus whose pottery suggests occupation from c. 3000 BC. Nearby is a large Bronze Age necropolis (c. 2000-1800 BC) with hundreds of tombs, excavated by John Myres in 1913 and by the Swedish Cyprus Expedition in 1927-1931, which yielded beak-spouted jugs and copper and bronze weapons.

lugares/saruq-al-hadid/resumen.texto: A site in the emirate of Dubai, about 40 km inland, occupied continuously from the Umm an-Nar period (2600-2000 BC) through the Iron Age, with fields of copper, bronze and iron smelting slag. Its greatest flourishing was in Iron II (1100-600 BC); the lack of water, fuel and ore on the site suggests religious motives.

lugares/ras-al-jinz/resumen.texto: A headland on the east coast of Oman, the easternmost point of the Arabian Peninsula, with a Bronze Age port (c. 2200-1900 BC) excavated since 1985 by a French-Italian team: a seven-room mudbrick building with workshops for shell, turtle shell and cosmetics. About 20% of the pottery came from the Indus valley, with transport jars and sherds bearing signs of the Indus script, and there is bitumen with reed impressions from the ships called Magan ships, from the mid-third millennium BC.

lugares/saar/resumen.texto: A settlement and temple from the Dilmun period in Bahrain, discovered in 1977 and excavated in 1977-1979 and by the London-Bahrain Archaeological Expedition in 1990-1999. In the houses copper fishhooks made in Bahrain, bitumen imported from Mesopotamia, pearl oyster shells and several hundred seals were found; the temple is associated with the observation of the summer solstice.

lugares/tarut/resumen.texto: An island in the Arabian Gulf, in present-day Saudi Arabia, inhabited for more than 5000 years; it was a link between Mesopotamia, the Indus valley and the Arabian Peninsula, and modern sources place it at the heart of Dilmun from c. 3000 BC. In 1968 Danish archaeologists found pottery from c. 4500 and from 3000 BC.

lugares/tayma/resumen.texto: A large oasis in northwestern Saudi Arabia, on the route between South Arabia and the eastern Mediterranean. Its first sedentary occupation dates to the early 4th millennium BC; by the middle of the second millennium it had expanded and was surrounded by a wall of mudbrick and sandstone, and in the Iron Age there is monumental architecture linked to Ramesside Egyptian hegemony.

lugares/jebel-buhais/resumen.texto: A rocky outcrop and necropolis in Sharjah, with tombs from the Neolithic (5000-4000 BC) through the Iron Age. It has beehive tombs of the Hafit period (3200-2600 BC), without human remains from that time, and Wadi Suq tombs; the Umm an-Nar period is not represented there, though it is in nearby Mleiha.

lugares/amman-citadel/resumen.texto: The hill of Amman, inhabited since the Neolithic and fortified in the Bronze Age, around 1800 BC. Excavations found Middle Bronze Age occupation (1650-1550 BC) in a tomb with pottery and scarabs; after 1200 BC it was the capital of the kingdom of Ammon.

lugares/tel-zeror/resumen.texto: A tell on the coastal plain of Israel, sometimes identified with Zror, a city conquered by Thutmose III, or with Machtar. Its Middle Bronze IIA city had a wall with a ditch; the site seems to have been abandoned from the 18th century BC and was not resettled until the early 15th century BC.

lugares/tell-el-farah-sur/resumen.texto: A tell in the western Negev, little occupied from the Middle Bronze IIB-IIC/III (c. 1600 BC), with fortifications, a gate and a ditch, and considered a Hyksos settlement. William F. Albright identified it with Sharuhen, the city that appears in Egyptian and biblical sources; others propose other identifications.

lugares/tell-judaidah/resumen.texto: One of the largest excavated sites in the Amuq Valley, with occupation from the Neolithic (c. 6000 BC) to the Byzantine period. Its crucibles with copper-tin crusts point to alloying around 4500 BC, and a mudbrick wall on stone foundations was dated by radiocarbon to around 3000 BC.

lugares/templo-de-hadad-de-alepo-lugar/r.texto: A temple of the storm god Hadad on the citadel hill of Aleppo, mentioned in cuneiform texts from Ebla and Mari. It was in use from the 24th century BC until at least the 9th century BC, according to the reliefs found by Kay Kohlmeyer; Aleppo was the «city of Hadad» and the capital of Yamhad.

lugares/tell-keisan/resumen.texto: A tell in northern Israel, large and prosperous in the Early and Middle Bronze Ages, with a glacis and a stone wall. In the Late Bronze Age the settlement was much smaller, and there is a destruction level from the beginning of the 12th century BC.

lugares/achziv/resumen.texto: A fortified Canaanite city on the north coast of Israel, settled from the 18th century BC; excavations found occupation from the Middle Bronze IIB to the early Middle Ages. The Bible names it Achzib.

lugares/tel-mevorakh/resumen.texto: A tell on the coast of Israel with a major occupation in the Middle Bronze IIB, excavated by Ephraim Stern in 1973-1976. In the Middle Bronze IIB it had a high earthen rampart and a fortress or garrison at the center, in use until the end of that period.

lugares/tel-michal/resumen.texto: A site on the central coast of Israel, near Herzliya, first settled at the end of the Middle Bronze IIB (1800/1750-1550 BC), with a 4 m high raised platform made of alternating layers of red clay and sand.

lugares/templo-de-los-obeliscos/resumen.texto: A Middle Bronze Age temple at Byblos, built around 1600 BC over the L-shaped temple of c. 2600 BC, with obelisks and standing stones in a courtyard around the cella; the obelisk of Abishemu, from c. 1800 BC, bears an Egyptian hieroglyphic inscription. Maurice Dunand excavated the site between 1924 and 1973.

lugares/necropolis-real-de-biblos/resume.texto: Nine shaft-and-chamber tombs of the Bronze Age, with sarcophagi of the city's kings, in a cliff at Byblos. The first three held Egyptian gifts bearing the names of Amenemhat III and Amenemhat IV, and Pierre Montet dated them to the 12th dynasty (19th century BC).

lugares/templo-de-diraz/resumen.texto: A Dilmun temple in the village of Diraz, in Bahrain, dated by its finds to around the third millennium BC; it is not known which god it was dedicated to, and its architecture has no parallels in Bahrain, Mesopotamia or the Indus.

lugares/al-sufouh/resumen.texto: A site in Dubai with scattered areas of occupation by the people of Magan; excavations in 1994-1995 found a circular Umm an-Nar-type tomb of 2500-2000 BC, 6.5 m in diameter, with individual burials, vessels, bronze weapons and beads.

lugares/tel-burna/resumen.texto: A tell in the Shephelah, beside the Guvrin Wadi, near Lachish and Gath, founded in the Early Bronze II and occupied in the Middle Bronze, the Late Bronze and the Iron Age. In the Late Bronze IIB (13th century BC) it reached its greatest extent, with a cult structure of 500 m².
